speechtext:
Yesterday the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) raised a question of privilege in connection with certain remarks made by the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence) the day before. I indicated I would reserve my decision on that question of privilege and deal with it later. I think the appropriate time to deal with it is now.
In the first instance, the question of privilege relates to an interpretation of the remarks of the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham. Since his remarks were open to more than one interpretation, we did take some time yesterday, at which time I felt the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham clarified very explicitly the intent of his remarks. As a result, I feel I must accept that the clarification extends back to the time the original remarks were made. Therefore, with that clarification in mind, it puts me in some serious doubt as to whether a question of privilege exists.
In addition, I have grave reservations as to whether an allegation about the staff of the House of Commons, important as it may be, in fact constitutes a question of privilege concerning the members of the House of Commons. In any case, I am not required to decide either of those matters because the hon. member did not follow up his question of privilege with a specific motion, and for this reason no action is called for by the Chair. In any case, after hearing the clarification offered by the hon. member, I have decided against finding a prima facie case of privilege under these circumstances.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege; it is, perhaps, not a major one but it affects the rights of all hon. members and it is one which I feel creates a bad impression.
For many weeks I have been interested in the report commissioned by the Minister of Transport pursuant to section 14(5) of the Pilotage Act and entitled the Desjardins report. I have brought the matter up with the Minister of Transport on various occasions in this chamber as well as in the standing committee. I have asked for this report and I have also asked for information regarding the cost of its preparation as well as the cost of a similar one called the Marler report which was commissioned last year. I have not received this information though I wrote on November 6 asking the minister specifically whether he was in a position to let me have a copy of the Desjardins report.
It has come to my attention within the last two hours that the Desjardins report is in the hands of several solicitors in Toronto and Montreal, and to the best of my knowledge it has neither been tabled in this House nor officially released by the minister elsewhere.
With the greatest respect to the minister, and to yourself, Mr. Speaker, I suggest the omission to furnish a member of parliament with a report in these circumstances constitutes a breach of privilege. If Your Honour should find that I do have a valid question of privilege, I would move:
That the Desjardins Report be tabled immediately pursuant to the rules of this House since it has been released, in effect, to the public.

speakeroldname: Hon. Daniel J. MacDonald (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF VISIT TO CANADIAN WAR GRAVES IN ITALY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to announce that plans have been made for an official Canadian delegation to visit Italy next April and May to hold commemorative ceremonies in the Canadian war cemeteries. My colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, has advised me that the government of Italy has enthusiastically concurred in the proposed visit.
The delegation will be headed by myself and I will be joined, on arrival in Rome, by His Excellency, our ambassador to Italy. It will be composed of representatives of the government, of the veterans organizations and of survivors of the 1st Canadian Corps who participated in the Italian campaign. This corps was in action during the period from July, 1943 to February, 1945 and involved more than 92,000 Canadian troops. More than 5,000 of them were killed or died of wounds and are buried in the Canadian cemeteries in Italy.
I am sure I do not have to remind hon. members of this House of the significance to Canada of names like Ortona, the Moro River, Rimini, the Liri Valley and the Gothic Line. These are names that will be remembered forever in our history with both pride and sorrow.
We will be holding memorial services at most of our war cemeteries in that country and, in addition, wreaths will be laid in a number of Italian war cemeteries, as the proposed dates for this visit include the thirtieth anniversary of the liberation of Italy.
My departmental officials will be contacting the commanding officers of the perpetuating units of the 1st Canadian Corps through their regimental and corps' asso-

ciations for the names of those who will be included in the survivor's portion of the delegation.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF VISIT TO CANADIAN WAR GRAVES IN ITALY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure this is one statement on motions on which members of the House will hear no controversy. My only comment is that members from all opposition parties, especially those who served in Italy, could have been included in the delegation. However, I commend the minister on what I think is a significant happening, a memorial service in Italy as an extension to our Remembrance Day ceremony here in Ottawa and across Canada. In view of the fact that 5,000 of our war heroes died of wounds in Italy, this ceremony may be able to reflect their memory for their parents or loved ones who remain in Canada. I commend the minister for the thought behind this visit and I wish him and his colleagues well on their voyage.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF VISIT TO CANADIAN WAR GRAVES IN ITALY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to join with the spokesman of the official opposition in commending the minister for leading this delegation to Italy on behalf of his department and these survivors. I am glad he included survivors of the liberation of Italy. I think all those who had the opportunity of attending memorial services which were held several years ago on a similar expedition to northern Europe came back with a better understanding and certainly an appreciation of the job that is being done, not only by Canada and some of the countries with which we were associated, but by all countries belonging to the war graves protocol.
Seeing the care that has been given some of the graves of the fallen provokes a sympathetic sentiment in the minds of loved ones toward that ceremony. I, too, also hope that the representation is made as broad as possible, particularly the representation of those who participated in the Italian campaign, and that as many as possible are given the opportunity to join the minister.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF VISIT TO CANADIAN WAR GRAVES IN ITALY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, doubtless our military personnel who risked their lives on the Italian battlefield during that World War, who are still living today, as well as the families of those who gave up their lives to liberate Italy, will be happy to hear today that the minister has decided to organize a delegation to commemorate the 30th anniversary of that liberation.
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that during those demonstrations, it will not be necessary to set up police security of the same magnitude as that we are now witnessing in Rome during the World Food Conference. Our delegation will be much more welcomed, and accepted, I am sure, under those circumstances.
I would like to add, however, that the minister should consider, if he has not already done so, the possibility of including in that delegation the Standing Committee of the House on Veterans Affairs which study those matters.
Mr. Speaker, I am convinced all Canadians would willingly accept that decision. We wish the delegation a good trip and express the hope that it will help somehow to improve our relations with Italy, though they have always been good.

subsubtopic: WORLD FOOD CONFERENCE IN ROME-POSSIBLE CONDITIONAL NATURE OF COMMITMENT TO SUPPLY ONE MILLION TONS OF GRAIN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. In view of the report that the Minister of Agriculture has taken the position that paying for the full one million tons of food aid in the current year in addition to the 650,000 tons to which Canada allegedly is already committed would be too costly for Canada to bear alone, I should like to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs whether the Government of Canada now proposes to contribute one million tons in the current year on top of the alleged 650,000 tons already committed or whether the pledge made in respect of the commitment by the minister of one million tons this year and in each of the following two years, a total of three years, is now conditional in some way upon foreign financial support in meeting part of this cost to Canada or whether the commitment for that one million tons in each of the three years is still unconditional as we were led to believe last week.

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: WORLD FOOD CONFERENCE IN ROME-POSSIBLE CONDITIONAL NATURE OF COMMITMENT TO SUPPLY ONE MILLION TONS OF GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the commitment with regard to the three year period is unconditional. It applies not to the current year but to the subsequent three years. That commitment is firm and involves an amount of one million tons per year. Under discussion at the present time

at the World Food Conference is the apparent shortfall in the present supply of grain to meet current requirements. There is some doubt, some uncertainty at present, as to the extent of that shortfall. The range of uncertainty is in the millions of tons, and discussions are continuing to determine exactly what the shortfall will be. We have already committed 650,000 tons for the current year, and the proposals coming forward are for an additional commitment. We have not yet made a specific response to that. What we have said is that Canada, in concert with other nations, would do its share to meet the current shortfall. We believe that it is appropriate at this point that other nations put money on the table in line with the very extensive commitments which Canada has already made. When nations are ready to move in concert, Canada's response will be immediate and positive.

subsubtopic: WORLD FOOD CONFERENCE IN ROME-POSSIBLE CONDITIONAL NATURE OF COMMITMENT TO SUPPLY ONE MILLION TONS OF GRAIN
speechtext: The government of Canada has not made any additional commitments for the current year, I understand, over and above what has already been committed, namely, some 650,000 tons. The government of Canada has not committed an additional bushel or ton of grain in the current year. I should like to ask the minister whether, when he speaks of other countries putting forward some concrete, tangible proposal of aid themselves, he has in mind a contribution toward meeting Canada's additional costs, if Canada contributes additional wheat, which seems to have been suggested by the Minister of Agriculture in Rome. Has the minister in mind that Canada will not make an additional commitment for the current year until other countries, perhaps the oil rich countries, make a firm commitment in some other areas, for food but not related to Canada's grain?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: WORLD FOOD CONFERENCE IN ROME-POSSIBLE CONDITIONAL NATURE OF COMMITMENT TO SUPPLY ONE MILLION TONS OF GRAIN

There are a number of separate proposals before the conference. One is with respect to the fund for agricultural development. There has been some expectation, not yet realized in the form of concrete amounts, that the oil producing countries might undertake participation in such an agricultural development fund. Canada stands ready to participate in that as well. It stands ready to participate in additional food commitments for this year. But in the light of the very substantial commitments which Canada has already made into the future, it seems to me that it is wise not to commit ourselves to an additional $200 million this year, in line with the suggestion made by the Leader of the Opposition, until we exert every possible persuasive effort on other countries to come forward and assist in the resolution of the world food crisis. On both fronts Canada is taking a very positive attitude.
I have already indicated in my statement in Rome that there was an additional commitment of $50 million for the current year that would be made available-

In
attempting to keep this subject within some orderly form of debate, I think the responsibility falls on the official opposition to make known to the committee of the whole the general thrust of our intent. In my opening remarks yesterday on clause 2, I indicated my concern about the position of the prerogatives of the Crown. I asked the minister if he would take up this subject with the law officers of the Crown, not on the basis of examining constitutional legislative authority but on the narrow question of the prerogatives of the Crown in right of the federal authority and the prerogatives of the Crown in right of the provinces. He promised to do so. As part of that discussion, I wish to move into the question of how, as members of this House, we can protect the Queen from harm. The amendments we wish to put forward are to clause 3, clause 36, clause 49 and clause 52(1).
We want to enshrine in the legislation the principle of consultation before any policy is determined. If one accepts the principle of consultation and agreement by enshrining it into the legislation, then there can be no question about the Queen in right of the province being harmed. In other words, if the provinces, on the advice of the Queen, accept this agreement after consultation with the federal government, then the interest of the Crown at both levels is the same.
I should like now to read the amendments I intend to put forward at the appropriate time, in order that members, by reading Hansard, can follow these proposals and consider them as a unified approach by Her Majesty's Official Opposition in its attempt to protect the Crown on the matter of prerogatives. Having read the proposed amendment to clause 3 last night, I would now read our further amendments into the record and then direct my remarks to the proposed amendment to clause 3.

That clause 36 of the bill on page 15 be amended by deleting lines 10 to 16 and substituting therefor the following:

The next proposed amendment is to clause 49, as follows: That clause 49 on page 20 be amended by deleting line 25 and substituting therefore the following:

The next amendment we propose to move on the question of enshrining the consultation process into the legislation is to clause 52(1), as follows:

"Governor in Council may, by regulation, subject to confirmation by order in council issued by the government of the producer-province concerned and having regard to the matters mentioned in subsection 51(2), prescribe prices for the various kinds of gas to which this part applies that are produced, extracted, recovered or manufactured in that province."
I should like to close my remarks at this time on clause 3, which reads:
This act is binding on Her Majesty in right of Canada and in right of any province.
As a layman, I say frankly that I am concerned about how this legislature, at the federal level, can combine the Queen both in right of the federal government and in right of several provinces in the same clause. Surely it is selfevident to a layman that before you can bind Her Majesty in right of the federal government, there should be some indication by the minister that this matter has been brought before the Governor General, who has given the consent of the Queen in respect of the right to discuss the terms of this bill. The minister has not yet indicated that he intends to present the consent of the Crown to this House, which is traditional when dealing with the prerogatives of the Queen.
The second question is even more dubious. How can this legislature, without any evidence before it that the Queen in right of any province has given her consent, give to our executive the powers which some of these clauses do which materially affect, directly or by incidence, the property of the Queen in right of any of the provinces? I think these questions are an indication of our legitimate concern and must be answered by the minister with evidence that he has consulted the law officers of the Crown as to

whether it is possible to bind Her Majesty in right of Canada and in right of the provinces, at the same time in the same bill, without any evidence of consent from Her Majesty being given either to this House or to the provinces.
I hope I have made it clear that it is beyond the capacity of most of us in this House to give a clear answer to this type of question. I simply point out to the minister, as I did yesterday, that if we passed this legislation as it is drafted and a province or an individual took it to court and the court ruled the legislation to be ultra vires in respect of some of its clauses regarding the prerogatives of Her Majesty, then this legislature would be the laughingstock of the country.
Yesterday I used an example which the minister was not sure was relevant. In that case, the federal legislature proceeded on the assumption of certain rights which it had in respect of Indian lands, and 40 years later a court decision ruled that the federal government was wrong, that it did not have the full right to alienate these lands and these lands should revert back according to the law and the prerogatives of the Queen in right of the province.
I suggest that it would be prudent for us to take a good, hard look at clause 3. Last night I read to the committee a proposed amendment to this clause which could make this legislation binding on Her Majesty in right of Canada and in right of any province. I repeat that we have had no evidence in the House that the Queen has given her consent to this legislation in right of any province. To make sure that we do not blunder on this point, I will repeat the amendment we propose to make sure that the federal legislation is sound.
That clause 3 of the bill on page 2 be amended by deleting line 9 and substituting therefor the following:
"province; and, where the legislative authority of the Parliament of Canada does not extend to bind Her Majesty in right of a province, then to the extent that Her Majesty in right of a province consents thereto."
I think what I am trying to do is clear. I would like the reaction of the minister on this point.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE ADMINISTRATION OF INTERPROVINCIAL, EXPORT AND IMPORT TRADE IN PETROLEUM AND PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as I indicated to the hon. gentleman yesterday and as he may recall from experience, the tendering of a bill to the House of Commons by a minister of the Crown is undertaken only after taking the advice of the law officers of the Crown- of course, the law officers of the Crown are the Minister of Justice and the Solicitor General-not only with regard to the legal efficacy of the words of the legislation but also their constitutionality. I heard that the hon. gentleman said outside the House there had not been consultation with the Department of Justice. I can assure him that in this case the bill was considered by the representatives of the department from the standpoint of the effectiveness of what is proposed and constitutionality.
The hon. gentleman raised the question of the consent of Her Majesty the Queen. In a measure of this kind, the consent of Her Majesty the Queen is given in this House in not one, but two ways. It is given, first, by the recommendation in this bill. His Excellency the Governor General has recommended to this House of Commons the present measure respecting the administration of inter-provincial, export and import trade in pretroleum and petroleum
November 14, 1974

products. So Her Majesty the Queen, by her legal representative here, has in effect recommended this bill.
Further, in respect of this, as in respect of other legislation, parliament is a trinity made up of this House of Commons, the Senate and the Queen in parliament. So the act of royal assents which so many members have often regarded as a formality, really is assent by Her Majesty the Queen, through her representative in the other place, indicating that she consents, as one of the three parts of parliament, to the legislative measure being enacted. In this regard, the royal assent in relation to the Queen in right of Canada is given in that way.

speechtext: On a point of information, Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether the minister would tell us if the counter-proposition applies, that Her Majesty in right of a province, in other words, being the legislature and the Crown, gives assent to a bill binding the Crown of Canada, and by doing so Her Majesty agrees that the Crown of Canada in right of Canada shall be bound.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE ADMINISTRATION OF INTERPROVINCIAL, EXPORT AND IMPORT TRADE IN PETROLEUM AND PRODUCTS
speechtext:
This is the question raised by the hon. gentleman yesterday. Of course, under our constitutional system, as the hon. member may not be aware, we have responsibility for distribution of the overall sovereignty of the country into provincial and federal governments. With regard to the rights extended to the Crown in right of Canada by the British North America Act, of course the royal assent is given to acts which fall within the competency of this parliament, in this particular case by the attendance of Her Majesty's representative in the other place.
The procedure followed in the legislature of a province would, of course, relate and be confined to its power and the constitutional authority given to the provincial government. Of course, the next question to be raised is, what about the interface between the two? The hon. member has asked to what extent the Queen in right of a province can be bound by this kind of a measure. That important constitutional question was decided long ago by the judicial committee of the Privy Council, for the reasons I indicated in response to the hon. member yesterday. It has been decided in relation to that commodity, both in relation to Canadian political history and Canadian constitutional history, which has been of such fundamental importance, namely, liquor.
I refer to the case of The Attorney General of British Columbia v. The Attorney General of Canada, reported in 1924 Appeal Cases at page 222. In that case the judicial committee pointed out that indeed the Crown in right of Canada could impose taxation on provincial property, as it could on the property of a private individual. In this particular case-I think this is the point the hon. member was raising-the Crown in right of Canada, when acting within the legislative powers conferred upon it by the B.N.A. act, can indeed bind and affect the property of the provincial government acting as a provincial government in the same way as with the property of a private individual in any province. In that sense we, by royal assent in this parliament-through the assent given on behalf of Her Majesty by her vice regal representative-
Oil and Petroleum
have the assent required for legislation here; and that assent, extending as it does to the legislative jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada, would bind the Crown in right of the province.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE ADMINISTRATION OF INTERPROVINCIAL, EXPORT AND IMPORT TRADE IN PETROLEUM AND PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I understand that we are permitted to speak on clause 2 even though there have been some interjections on clause 3 and other clauses. I should like to make a few remarks in a general way at this stage concerning Bill C-32 which, as I have said before, proposes a quartet of government of Canada proposals governing the petroleum industry in Canada which I feel is part of a general program which will create a shortage of oil and natural gas in this country before too long.
Questions were put to the minister yesterday regarding the supply situation in Canada. The minister could not answer them because he had not cleared the matter with some of the producing provinces or had not received any reaction from them. I believe the report of the National Energy Board will show that we have already reached the peak of our ability to produce and that we will be facing a period of shortage commencing in three or four years. I think this is a very serious matter for Canada. The government is adopting a sort of "fat cat" approach to the problem; it is taking a very short-sighted and short-term approach. The government is trying to appeal to the consumers of the country on a short-term basis by keeping prices in tight restraint, without giving any indication whether there will be any incentives for the producers or finders of petroleum to enable them to make a profit. I am very sorry that the government is attacking the profit motive in this area of our endeavours because, in my opinion, there is nothing wrong with making a decent, honest profit, particularly after many years of investment with very little return.
The second part of the proposals will be in the budget which we will hear next Monday night. The third part will be in the PetroCan legislation which will be coming in the new year. The fact is that the government does not seem to be able to make up its mind regarding the ground rules for the development of petroleum and petroleum products off our shores and in the Arctic area of the country. I refer to the land use regulations. It appears that over-all we have a package of proposals that creates a great deal of uncertainty.
The measure before us deals with price restraint and price control which, if it is allowed to continue, can only lead to a shortage of oil. That brings to mind the fact that this legislation results primarily from the so-called agreement of March 27 in which the first ministers of this country agreed to a limited period of price control for crude oil. This government, however, has seen fit to bring forth a document, Bill C-32, which flies in the face of that agreement by seeking to give the government power to control the price of crude oil and natural gas for an indefinite period, on a permanent basis. This is being done under the guise of powers granted under the B.N.A. Act in the area of regulation of trade and commerce.
However, I suggest that this grasping for power demonstrates the poor bona fides of the government and the actual dishonesty of its approach when it attempts to set the wellhead price of crude oil and natural gas under this legislation. I think the government would have more cred-

November 14, 1974
Oil and Petroleum
ibility if its power was restricted to interprovincial trade in oil and natural gas, but when it reaches inside the producing provinces to control the wellhead price I think it goes well beyond its constitutional powers.
This bill deals with many other aspects than just fixing and controlling the price of natural gas and crude oil. The powers which the federal government seeks would allow its agents or officers to enter the offices of provincial governments to conduct searches and seize documents. I do not believe that this can be considered a power granted to the federal government under the guise of regulating interprovincial trade. That is why I think the ideas expressed by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain have merit and should be considered by the minister more seriously than they have to date.
It seems to me that the minister justifies price control under this bill as being a power granted to the government in respect of the regulation of trade and commerce. However, under that umbrella the minister brings in all sorts of other things. Here I differ somewhat from the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain, in that he wishes to make this a better bill, while I do not think it is a good bill, nor do I think it can be made better so long as the federal government wishes to use it as a tool to discriminate against and penalize the oil producing areas of this country.
As I said before, this bill represents a continuation of the government's "fat cat" approach. It may be very popular and it may make the government appear to be a hero in Vancouver, Toronto and Montreal, but I wonder how popular the government will be four or five years from now when those areas will suffer from a shortage of petroleum products-because that shortage will come just as sure as night follows day, if we do not have a proper price and some certainty injected into the industry. If the price is not right, we will not have the power.
I think the possible consequence of the present figures should filter through the skulls of members across the aisle who are responsible in this area. All figures indicate that drilling and exploration activity has decreased, largely because of the prospect of this legislation and the government's budgetary proposals which will be revealed on Monday. For example, drilling activity is down by 7 per cent in Alberta and 75 per cent or 76 per cent in Saskatchewan. In the United States, drilling activity has increased by more than 20 per cent. These figures show what is happening in this country. Clearly, the aims of this bill should be changed; it should be amended. This law must be so administered as to ensure adequate supplies for Canada. The bill as presently worded will not assure adequate supplies. Its main thrust is keeping prices at a minimum level, and that policy is short-sighted.
As I said earlier, the agreement made by the first ministers on March 27 was to expire at the end of June, 1975. In conformity with that agreement, should not controls envisaged under this bill also expire at the end of June, 1975, because that was the time limit for the original agreement? There should be a new agreement to take care of provincial rights. The government would be more credible if it included in the bill a schedule showing the level

to which prices shall rise. I understand that the government supports a policy of staged price increases for the foreseeable future. Oil prices are to approach world commodity price levels. It is government policy to prevent this from happening suddenly. The government wants a cushion which will allow the Canadian economy to adapt gradually to price increases. If that is the government's intention, it is not evident from the language of this bill. Instead, the bill seems designed to keep prices at the lowest possible level.
If the government intends to increase prices, it should say so now in order to clear away uncertainties and show its thinking. As the hon. member for Calgary Centre said, we would all feel more comfortable if we could see the minister's intentions in writing. Let me add, I would feel more comfortable if they were in sworn form, as he has been fast and loose with promises he has made to various people in this field, both in the provinces and in industry, during past months. In my view, the bill should distinguish between old and new oil. I contend that if old and new oil are treated in the same way, any incentive for finding new oil will be lacking. Those who drill wells at great risk and find new oil should be allowed a greater return on their investment. That would encourage exploration for oil. Of course, at present that incentive is lacking.
The people in my area doubt the government's ability to deal with our difficulties. If you consider our history, you will see that until 1930 the oil producing areas of this country were under federal control. Not until 1930 did Alberta and Saskatchewan acquire jurisdiction over and ownership of their oil resources. During the first 63 years of our history there was no great development of oil resources in this country and any development which took place was accompanied with great economic waste. Millions of cubic feet of natural gas were lost in Alberta because of faulty or negligently drawn federal conservation measures. Once the provinces gained control of their resource it did not take them long to introduce sensible and useful conservation measures which, according to many, are the best in the world. These measures were not drawn up by some Big Daddy in Ottawa. The federal government is now trying to take back what it gave 44 years ago. I find that discouraging.
Logically, the government's policies will force the provinces to nationalize their petroleum industries. I notice that Eric Kierans, in his speech to the Canadian Tax Foundation in Toronto the other day suggested this. I do not often agree with that gentleman, but I must agree with what he said. It seems to me that the only alternative left to the rightful owners of this resource is nationalization of the industry. The federal government then will not be in a position to levy taxes on the industry, as it is now.
What I am suggesting is not without precedent. In the last 15 years, practically all private electrical generating plants have come under provincial ownership. The only exception is the electrical industry in Alberta, and this exception was made possible because the federal government, in 1965 or 1966, changed its tax policies and allowed a portion of corporate taxes which would be paid by such private electrical generating companies to be returned to the consumers. Without that concession such companies
November 14, 1974

could not be economically viable; they could not compete with provincial companies which do not have to pay income tax. So one can see the influence of federal government budgetary and fiscal policies upon certain private industries in the provinces.
I suppose the present measure is an outgrowth of the Prime Minister's outlook. He has written somewhere, I think, that provincial governments are useful for establishing the beachheads of socialism in this country. He now leads the federal government, and I suppose he wants to make sure this bill will be instrumental in the establishment of beachheads at the provincial level. That would appear to be the practical result of this major federal government policy.
During the clause by clause study the constitutionality of this bill should be put to the test. The minister should explain why the consent of the provincial Crown representatives is not necessary. I heard his explanation a few minutes ago; it certainly does not satisfy me. It may become apparent that this bill is not as constitutionally valid as the minister thinks. During the clause by clause study we should pay particular attention to writing into this bill the provision that it must be concerned with creating and maintaining a supply of petroleum products for the whole country. We must get away from the restrictive approach that is now in the bill, as it can only result in a man-made shortage of oil and natural gas in our country by the end of this decade.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to ask the minister two questions. If Your Honour agrees, I will ask them separately. Yesterday the minister made reference to the fact that reductions in the export of oil to the United States would, of necessity, reduce the amount of revenue which would accrue to the export tax fund, but that this might not be offset by a reduction in imports because it would not be possible to ship oil to the area east of the Ottawa Valley until the pipeline was completed. In consequence, there would be a period of time when the surplus oil in western Canada would have to be stored or left in the ground. We could be importing almost as much as we would be exporting. Consequently, the compensation payments would be very heavy in view of the fact that revenue from the export tax would be reduced.
We will be able to discuss this bill much better if the minister will give us some information about the proposed pipeline to eastern Canada. It is almost a year since the Prime Minister announced that the government intended to have the pipeline built so that western Canadian crude could find its way into the Montreal market. I notice from a press report in this morning's newspaper that discussions have apparently been completed between the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and Interprovincial Pipe Line. It is suggested that a number of options are being examined. Apparently Interprovincial Pipe Line wants a guarantee that there will be sufficient throughput in the line to meet their operating costs and to retire their capital investment.
A number of suggestions have been made. First, the government should guarantee a specific amount of reve-
Oil and Petroleum
nue to Interprovincial Pipe Line. Second, there should be a change in the tariff structure for the whole of the existing pipeline from Edmonton to Toronto and Sarnia. Third, the federal government might build the pipeline from Sarnia to Montreal and operate it, or a northern pipeline through northern Ontario and northern Quebec. Fourth, federal government might build a pipeline and lease it back to Interprovincial Pipe Line. Interprovincial, in turn, would buy the pipeline out of payments for the oil throughput. In that way the pipeline would eventually become the property of Interprovincial Pipe Line.
In view of the urgency of this matter, I would ask the minister whether the cabinet has made any decision as to which of these or any other propositions have been agreed upon. If a decision has not been reached, can the minister give us some idea as to how soon a decision will be reached? Can the minister give the committee any timeframe with regard to the earliest possible date for commencement of construction, and an approximate date when the pipeline is expected to be completed? This information will certainly have an effect on the compensation payments and the export charge fund. If the minister could give us some idea, it would be helpful. It would also be helpful to those who live east of the Ottawa Valley. If there is any embargo this winter, there will certainly be a good deal of fear and apprehension on the part of people who live in eastern Canada regarding assured supplies of oil. Therefore, any statement the minister can make on this point will be helpful. I would like to ask the minister that question now and then, if I may, Mr. Chairman, ask my second question later.

Mr. Chairman, with regard to the pipeline and the hon. member's request that I review the record and give a current statement, he will recall the government indicated its wish that the pipeline be extended to Montreal in September of last year. Following that indication and discussions with Interprovincial Pipe Line, the company engaged in a study of the route, a survey of the route and an analysis of the requirements. In due course it presented an application to the National Energy Board as it is required to do by law. That application, which was made this spring, had to be adjourned because of the intervention of the government of Quebec which objected to the route the company proposed to follow for the pipeline as it approached within 50 miles of the island of Montreal, particularly with relation to environmental risks created in this regard.
I think I would be correct in saying that the view of the board was that the environmental concerns were appropriately expressed. The company thereupon went back to work and planned a new route which would meet the objections of the Quebec government. It came forward to the board again in the autumn with a new plan for a changed route to meet the environmental requirements. The hope had been that the original planning provided adequate time for the planning stage and approval. However, the intervention of the government of Quebec set that timetable back to this fall. In the meantime, opinions-expressed primarily by the industry-caused the company to be concerned about the possibility, not so much in the seventies but in the early eighties when the pipeline would be in operation, that depletion of the reser-

November 14, 1974
Oil and Petroleum
voir in western Canada might have reached a point where there would not be adequate throughput. The servicing of both the existing Canadian demand west of the Ottawa Valley line and the additional demand would be taken care of by the pipeline east of the Ottawa Valley line.
The company at that stage sought assurance that, having undertaken the financing and construction of the line, it would not find itself in financial difficulties if it had to bear the fixed operating costs of a project which, for the time being at least, might not be producing revenue. The government has been discussing this question with the company. I saw the report to which the hon. member referred and I can say that the statement that discussions have been completed is not true. In fact, there have been exchanges very recently concerning a possible solution to the difficulty about which the company has expressed concern. It is, of course, desirable to complete this line as soon as possible, but as well as security of supply we must take into account the element of the exposure of the consolidated revenue fund, in addition to the time necessary to investigate the environmental aspect involved.

speechtext:
I
agree with the minister that the matters raised with respect to possible environmental difficulties should be investigated and proper action taken. However, I cannot understand why, when the government and the company were discussing the construction of the line, and when the survey of the route was being made, these financial aspects were not considered at the same time. The fact that the minister cannot give us any timeframe within which construction will begin or be completed is bound to cause a great deal of dismay in the eastern part of Canada.
There is a second question I should like to ask. It has to do with a report that the Norwegian minister of foreign affairs has informed the International Energy Group in Brussels that Norway does not intend to sign the international energy agreement which is now before a committee of this House for discussion. Can the minister tell us whether or not this amounts to a complete rejection, or whether Norway is seeking some kind of associate status in the 12-nation group, as newspaper reports have indicated? Is it true that Norway does not favour the agreement because she expects soon to become an exporter of oil herself and does not, therefore, consider it appropriate for her to be a member of a group which, except for Canada, is made up entirely of oil importing countries? If that is the

reason, then it should surely make us pause and think about whether Canada should become a party to that agreement.
I do not wish to discuss the agreement now; there will be plenty of opportunity to do so when the committee reports back to the House. My own feeling is that the agreement is not a good one for Canada. All hon. members may not be of this opinion. However, the arguments I have been advancing in committee are strengthened by the fact that Norway does not feel she should be required to restrict her own consumption while at the same time continuing to export to other countries. I think time will show that the concern of those of us who have questioned the value of this agreement is fully justified. I do not think the Canadian people will ever be content with a situation in which they are asked to ration gasoline in this country while we continue to maintain normal exports of oil to the United States. This could happen under the agreement to which I have referred.
The minister has undertaken that the government will not sign this agreement until the report of the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works is dealt with in the House. That report may not come back to us for some time, so it would be useful if we could obtain this information. The minister may want to tell the committee what position the government is taking in light of the Norwegian government's stand and in light of the fact that the International Energy Group is pressing very hard for an immediate decision by Canada.

speechtext:
I thank the hon. gentleman for raising the question. First, with regard to the Norwegian decision I can confirm that the Norwegians have decided not to adhere to the agreement. One could perhaps speculate that this decision is not unconnected with the trauma they feel generally concerning their economic relations with other western European countries. I am referring to the discussions held with regard to their membership in the EEC. Specifically, though, their decision might have been taken because they anticipate that in the near future they will become net exporters of oil. Norway's position as a net exporter would, of course, be substantially different from that of Canada. Canada is a net exporter at the moment but we depend, of course, on imports from overseas to supply the eastern market, and this position is not likely to change for at least a decade.
So although Norway will be able to take care of its own needs from its offshore production, according to present expectation, there is no real prospect of this in Canada until 1988. In this sense our position is quite different from that of Norway. It is therefore important that we take steps to secure for the eastern half of Canada supplies which must enter this country from overseas, and for this reason we think we should become party to the agreement respecting the international quota program.
It has been suggested from time to time that there is a quality of belligerence in confrontation about membership in the IEG. I would just mention that while the Norwegians are not in, some of the traditional non-belligerents like Switzerland, Sweden and Austria have decided to come in, even though they were not originally participants in the ECG discussions.
November 14, 1974

The second comment I would make in answering the question as to where we stand is this: Because this matter is before parliament at the present time, because we have sought the response of the provincial governments, and because we have not yet received either the committee's reaction or the response of the provincial governments to the proposals, we are naturally reluctant to go ahead. Indeed, it would be improper to go ahead and commit ourselves to a definite adherence to the agreement. On the other hand, if the rhythm of participating in these discussions is dictated by states which, perhaps, do not have the constitutional complexity of Canada is that provisional adherence will be required in the very near future so that the discussions can continue, I have indicated to my colleagues, and they have agreed, that we should provisionally participate in the agreement, subject specifically to the proviso that Canada's participation is contingent upon constitutional requirements, and particularly upon parliament's reaction to the proposal.
One other comment I think I should make regarding the question of exports is this. I have been advised in this respect that the accurate description of the program is somewhat different from that given by one of my officials in committee. The opinion was advanced by an official before the committee that in the event of an emergency Canada would be proscribed from decreasing its exports to the United States. In a practical sense that would probably be the effect. However, I am now advised that Canada could indeed decide to reduce exports to the United States further, even in the event of an emergency, to meet its own needs; but the amount of such reduction in exports to the United States during the emergency would thereupon be deducted from the amount of oil we are entitled to receive from overseas. Thus, in those circumstances, since the matter would balance out, it is very likely that we would decide to keep the flow of oil continuing, in the expectation that oil would be delivered on the east coast. I think that is the only important change that I would make to the general presentation made in committee.

Mr. Chairman, I should just like to say a few words on the general terms of the bill and, in the time allotted to me, pose a few questions to the minister. I might say at the outset, though, that I find it very strange that we are debating this bill, studying it clause by clause, when so many uncertainties need to be cleared up. In reply to a question from a member in the House, the
Oil and Petroleum
minister said: "We are going to make a decision. We have until 1975 to decide whether or not we are going to enter into this agreement with 12 other countries regarding some kind of common front for the exportation of oil". To my mind, that is a very easy question to clear up. The minister should have reached that decision before presenting this bill to the House.
This bill is supposed to answer some of the uncertainties existing in the energy field in Canada, particularly uncertainties relating to oil and gas supply. For the last two years, countries of the world have been stepping up exploration of oil and gas but we have seen the direct opposite take place in Canada. Something like 50 per cent of Canada's potential drilling capacity has been withdrawn. Thirty-two rigs out of 320 can be equated with a rate of 10 per cent, but actually 50 per cent of our potential drilling capacity has been lost. A lot of smaller rigs have remained. Nevertheless, this situation is a shame. My first question is this: Will this bill right that shame? Will it bring about more certainty by bringing back into the oil and gas industry some degree of confidence and encouragement regarding further exploration?
I was not in the chamber yesterday afternoon when the minister made his speech; I was working in the agricultural committee studying a bill having to do with government intervention in the field of marketing grain, but I did read this afternoon the remarks the minister made and found no answer to that question. I think the minister owes it to the House, before we pass this bill, to give us an answer to the question: Will the bill in any way encourage further exploration for oil and gas in Canada? If so, what particular features of the bill will do this? In this regard I should like to quote from a telegram sent by the president of Imperial Oil. He says:
In its language and intent, the bill must reflect its transitional purpose. A specific expiry date-
In other words, the oil companies want to know when this bill will cease to have effect. In their minds, the provisions of this bill should only be temporary, as was Bill C-18. But the minister puts no expiry date in the bill. I continue:
A specific expiry date, which would ensure reconsideration of all sections of the bill, is essential.
Without these, Bill C-32 can only be read as a major obstacle facing the job of providing oil and gas for future Canadian needs.
That language is pretty clear, Mr. Chairman. This is one of the major oil exploration companies operating in Canada. In fact, this is the company that discovered Leduc No. 1, a company that is exploring for oil entirely on its own in the Mackenzie delta, a company that has done a great deal of what might be called wildcat drilling, which is really what we should ask oil companies to do, whether Imperial Oil or Canadian-owned companies like Home. This would enable us to discover oil and gas potential anywhere in Canada. Here we have one of the major wildcatters, a company that has had great experience, and I might say success, saying that this bill will be a major obstacle to providing Canada with its future oil and gas requirements.
I do not know how secure our reserves are, because the National Energy Board has not reported on them. We are being asked to deal with this bill with suspicion, with

I would take the minister's remarks in respect of the province of Alberta as being slightly disrespectful, and as an individual who is here from a part of Alberta to represent Alberta, I react to that disrespect as I should if I am to serve that area well. The prairie provinces have fought long and hard for constitutional acceptance of the fact that resources belong to the provinces. That decision was made some time ago, as far back as 1930. A royal commission was set up to study the matter, and the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan were awarded $5 million for the expenditure of their resources which had taken place prior to that date. That constitutional question has been settled.
Does the minister now feel that he can move in with this bill and arbitrarily set gas prices, deciding that Tran-sCanada PipeLines shall be the common carrier, maintaining a monopoly, with the price of gas set at whatever he wants? Does he really feel he can do that without destroying the constitutional arrangement decided on in 1930 in favour of the prairie provinces? I do not think he can really do so without first reaching some kind of agreement with the provinces. The minister clearly states at page 1297 of Hansard that he has not yet reached agreement with the provinces. Parliament would be making a colossal error in passing this bill without first allowing the provinces to reach agreement with this government, because constitutionally the matter of resources remains solely with the provinces.
Just recently Quebec announced its complete support for the Alberta position, and Newfoundland has always maintained the position that Alberta was right in this constitutional fight in respect of control of natural resources. One cannot dispute the fact that the minister, by clauses 3, 36, 38, 39 and 42 of this bill, does go against the constitutional position of the provinces. I have read what the minister said and he obviously refuses to face that question squarely. Apparently he believes this government is all-powerful and can move into the control of resources. The minister said in his remarks that by the establishment of the National Energy Board in 1959 the government in fact set the precedent which allowed him to move in. However, I suggest that no such power followed the establishment of the National Energy Board. The job of the National Energy Board is to assess and recommend to parliament certain action in respect of energy.

The minister can say that as a result of this bill he will be able to price oil cheaply in all regions of Canada. I suppose that is true as long as there is oil available, but there is no more heavy oil coming from Saskatchewan and northeastern Alberta. The industry has stopped producing heavy oil in those areas because refining costs are so high that it is not economical. a government project, I would like to think there would be some guarantee that it would be an economically sound project and not some pipe dream of the minister.
From reading the minister's remarks and listening to his answers to questions, it would seem that he has avoided more questions than he has answered. speechtext:
that Bill C-214, to amend the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill is a hardy veteran, this being the fourth or fifth time I have presented it. The idea first was brought forward as a notice of motion.
The bill is short.- It calls on Electoral Boundaries Commissions to give reasons for recommendations concerning changes in electoral boundaries. Recommendations for changes in constituency boundaries have not contained the reasons why commissioners made such changes.
If hon. members will cast their minds back, they will no doubt remember the last two occasions on which the provisions of the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act were to be invoked. Frankly, I can only say of that act that it is a minor, mitigated disaster. In many instances redistribution proposals were not satisfactory, and created a great deal of dissatisfaction. Actually the last attempt at redistribution created so much dissatisfaction on the part of members of the House that it was agreed to suspend the effects of redistribution until December 31, 1974. The recommendations of the past cannot be reinstituted. The commissions have changed, circumstances have changed, and it would be necessary to start all over again.

November 14, 1974
Electoral Boundaries
I want to see reasons attached to commission recommendations. At present members may comment upon recommendations but cannot amend those recommendations. Members may comment on those recommendations in this House, and then the commissioners may read what has been said and possibly amend their recommendations. However, experience shows that we wasted our time. The odd name has been changed, but that is about all, even though the general distribution scheme involved the wildest abortion, or totally unjust concepts, or an entirely false premise about the propriety of the suggested area of representation. I am speaking of the representation of people by representatives. The reports are almost always returned in their original form; sometimes they are mildly changed.
All members, I think, have had the opportunity of seeing preliminary reports and appearing at public hearings. I will not repeat what went on in Alberta in the last redistribution but there was universal condemnation of the proposals of the commissioners. I cannot see how these so-called independent commissions are protecting anything. They are doing a worse job than members themselves did in the past.
Be that as it may, I think the commissions can do a better job. But they could do a far better job if they would spell out the reasons for recommending particular changes. Let us know the principles which they apply within each province. I maintain that far too few commissions pay attention to demographic circumstance. Some of them tend to think in terms of numbers of votes, which has resulted in intolerable injustices.
In the last proposal in Alberta we saw rural constituencies with populations far larger than in urban constituencies. The results were fantastic and violated the principle of good representation. In other words, the public must have ready access to the member who represents them and he, in his turn, must have ready access to his constituents.
I am not talking about the difficulty of conducting elections. I wish that commissioners would occasionally become involved in election campaigns because then they would see how wrong are academic writers who blindly support the principles of the act, and how wrong headed are some newspaper editors who piously agree with some of the garbage written about the workings of the act. Only by fighting an election would they realize how stupid is our redistribution system.
As well, I think commissioners should be punished for some of their decisions by being made to service the constituencies they have drawn. In many cases that would be virtually impossible.

There is merely a map with lines on it, but no indication why any boundary was changed. Therefore I have brought forward this simple amending bill and ask the House to support it.
The motion before the House calls for this bill to be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections. I believe it should be sent to that committee, where the bill can be discussed at greater length than in the House. I believe the House is disposed to send the bill to that committee. Actually, it was suggested to me through the usual channels that, in order to allow as many members as possible to participate in the present debate, speeches in the House should be limited to 10 minutes. Either at six o'clock, or after the last member has spoken, I think there will be a disposition to send the bill to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections. I recommend it to the House.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING REASONS FOR COMMISSIONS' REPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 rise with pleasure to talk on this bill as, for the first time, I am in complete agreement with a member of the opposition. The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) argues persuasively.
The bill, which the hon. member indicated has been before the House on three previous occasions, is timely as the government has announced its intention to present new legislation which will affect electoral boundaries readjustment and redistribution. The bill which the government will be presenting will, of course, affect only the British North America Act. It will not deal specifically with the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act.
This bill is timely because the amendment which the hon. member for Edmonton West is presenting draws attention to the latter act. I would like to see this bill go to committee because I have a direct interest in the question of amending that act. Indeed, I intend to present a private member's bill which will seek to amend Section 13 of that act which, by reference, is the one in which the hon. member for Edmonton West is interested.
When the hon. member speaks of getting the commissioners to affix reasons to the readjustment they propose, he is in effect referring to Section 13 where the reasons are set down and the criteria are determined. These are the criteria that interest me as a member from Northern Ontario.
Section 13 sets down the subdivision or quotient for any given province, based upon the total population within that province and the number of seats allocated to it according to the provisions of the British North America Act. The amalgam method, which will be the subject matter of the proposed government bill, sets down the formula by which the numbers of seats in various provinces are to be amended. However, that bill does not deal with the division of these particular seats within any given province. As I understand it, there is no proposed amendment in the government legislation which will deal

with this provision of seats within a province. That is why I will be presenting a private member's bill.
Section 13 permits the commissioners under certain circumstances to augment the number of seats within a constituency, or reduce it, by 25 per cent from the provincial quotient. I will be presenting an amendment whereby the number of electors within a particular proposed boundary could be as much as 35 per cent less than the normal quotient within that province.
The reasons 1 will be presenting a bill is because I feel the present situation in the province of Ontario is very unfair to a certain portion of this province, that is, the northern one half or two thirds of the province of Ontario.
Under the redistribution which was presented to this House in June of last year there was a proposal to increase the number of seats in Ontario by three. However, there was a contemporaneous reduction in the number of northern Ontario seats by two, reducing the number of seats in northern Ontario from 12 to 10. Paradoxically, the whole of Ontario was to gain three seats, the net result being that the southern portion of the province would gain five additional seats over what it had prior to 1972. I objected to that position for very valid reasons.
I made a speech on this particular topic on July 5, and continued it on July 6, 1973. During that speech I stated the reasons why I felt consideration ought to be given by the commissioners to my proposal. I stated they should be permitted to increase or decrease the number of electors in one area up to 35 per cent below the normal quotient. I indicated that the provisions within the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act were very astute and complete in their consideration of the special factors that affect northern Ontario seats. I quote that particular section:
the commission may depart from the strict application of rules (a) and (b) in any case where
(i)	special geographic considerations, including in particular the sparsity, density or relative rate of growth of population of various regions of the province, the accessibility of such regions or the size or shape thereof, appear to the commission to render such a departure necessary or desirable, or
(ii)	any special community or diversity of interests of the inhabitants of various regions of the province appears to the commission to render such a departure necessary or desirable,
The northern portion of Ontario represents roughly two thirds of the total area of the province. Since World War II there has been a tendency toward greater centralization within urban areas. On information which is now available it is projected that by the year 2000, 90 per cent of the total Canadian population will be concentrated within urban centres.
Although we in this House may pride ourselves on being able to govern the affairs of this nation, the whole power of the body politic within Canada is subdivided. Jurisdictionally and constitutionally, we have the provinces and the federal government. No one will deny those governments are located in large urban centres and their deliberations and concerns are influenced by those centres.
Economic activities within a country have a great deal of influence on the government of that country. In turn, its economic activity is guided to a considerable extent by the corporate entities within the country. Those corporate entities are predominantly located in the large urban cen-
Electoral Boundaries
tres. That is where they have their head offices. They are motivated by the feelings generated within those large urban centres.
The press, which has a great deal of influence on the development of a country and on the opinion of the electorate, is primarily located in large urban centres. One need only listen to the complaints from western Canada relating to CBC newscasts. All news coverage is concentrated toward Toronto. The net effect is that a direction is given to our country which is really an urban direction.
The paradox is that we have four million square miles of territory. This four million square miles is, but for a very small percentage, occupied. If we are to encourage the development of this area we ought not to start by reducing the number of representatives which flow from it into the central locations. I would be very sorry to find that northern Ontario, which is rich in all that is now in demand on the international market, would find itself without representation. I would not like to see the exploitation of that area directed from the large urban centres.
I am looking at the hon. member for Parry Sound-Mus-koka (Mr. Darling). Although he is considered to be in southern Ontario, his problems are very similar to those being experienced in northern Ontario. He understands very well of what I speak, and is very sympathetic with the position I have taken.
I will conclude my remarks and hope this bill will pass with all dispatch. I will cite one of my early childhood heroes, the Prime Minister of this country in 1946, the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, when dealing with redistribution during the 1946 debate. He said:
Do we always realize that the area of this country is enormous-from one ocean to the other, from the boundaries of the United States to the North Pole, an area scarcely smaller than the whole of Europe and somewhat larger than the whole of the United States? Of course, were it not for the fact that only a relatively small fraction of it is regarded as potentially valuable for agricultural purposes, it would be difficult to explain why there are only twelve million people in that vast area; but the representation is territorial and the territory is very large.
He places this comment in the context of the criteria which should guide redistribution, and in his mind, a very lucid and far-seeing mind, he maintains that the primary consideration should be representation on the basis of territory. Representation by population is essential, and I agree we should keep as close as possible to that standard if we are to maintain our democratic principles. Nevertheless the element of territory is very real in Canadian history and it will become even more important in the future as we accept increasing numbers of immigrants, as our own population grows, and as we occupy territories which will then be ready for more intensive development.
I am pleased to support the hon. member for Edmonton-West. There may be other occasions upon which I shall be pleased to do so, though I cannot for the moment think of any.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is an interesting afternoon. First of all I am in the position of being able to congratulate the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) on what appears to be the second occasion within a couple of years

when he is winning something in private members' hour. A year to two ago a private member's resolution he introduced was referred to a committee, which was in itself a success, though I do not think it went any further.
