The other thing I find interesting this afternoon, something which almost leaves me speechless, is to hear the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Blais) supporting a bill brought in by a private member on the opposite side of the House. His usual role in private members' hour is to oppose or talk out anything which comes from this side. Mind you, though, when the hon. member from Edmonton West and the hon. member for Nipissing are agreed, I feel I should read the legislation again and make sure that something is not being put over on us.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING REASONS FOR COMMISSIONS' REPORTS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING REASONS FOR COMMISSIONS' REPORTS
speechtext:
Actually, Your Honour, I do not object to this bill. I am not wildly enthusiastic about it, but I do not object to it and I am prepared to go along with it on the understanding that it be given second reading and that the bill itself, not just the subject matter, be sent to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections. Because there are one or two things I would like to say in reply to remarks made by the hon. member for Edmonton West, I thought I would like to make it clear at the outset that I am prepared to support the bill.
I would like to say, Mr, Speaker, that I am unrepentant over the issue of redistribution by an independent commission. I have had plenty of experience of the old regime under which redistribution was done by a committee of this House. In effect, this meant it was done in the offices of some of the ministers-the key minister for each province really drew the map for that province, and the committee just went through the motions. I do not want to see us go back to that system and I am sure that nobody else does, either. Even those who are critical of the present method do not suggest we return to redistribution by the members of the House.
The constituencies belong to the people, to the country, and they are not ours to draw up or carve out, whichever figure of speech you want to use. For this reason, I wish to take a close look at the bill before us and be sure that it will not stymie or hurt the process of redistribution by an independent commission. I do not believe it does and, therefore, as I said before, I am prepared to go along with it. But I do not think this is an occasion for blasting away at the things the commissions have done.

The hon. member for Edmonton West said that the redistribution boundaries produced last time, the maps for which we received in 1973 or in 1974, created almost a rebellion on the part of hon. members. I know that in one or two provinces there were pretty strong feelings about the way the lines had been drawn, but for the most part the complaints made against that redistribution, and the complaints which resulted in legislation being introduced to postpone it, were not against the way the lines had been drawn by the commissioners it was because of the apportioning of the number of seats to each province as determined by the terms of the British North America Act.
So what members really were saying when they wished to put off redistribution at that time, was that they wished to look again at the formula for dividing the number of seats among the various provinces. I, too, think that the time has come when we should consider, if we retain a redistribution formula in which a floor is provided for areas such as the Yukon and Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Newfoundland, whether there are now other areas in this country which should also be protected.
However, I should not dwell on this issue because it is not the issue which is really before us today. I also want to affirm my belief that to have an independent commission do the job of redistribution is a much better way. I know that in the case of Alberta there has, in the past, been a good deal of feeling about the boundaries, but generally speaking I think the commissioners have done a pretty reasonable job. The last one, the one that has been put off, hurt me as far as my own constituency was concerned. As a matter of fact, it wiped it right out by name.
I am glad to see the hon. member for Edmonton West shaking his head at that remark.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING REASONS FOR COMMISSIONS' REPORTS
speechtext: They can't wipe you out.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING REASONS FOR COMMISSIONS' REPORTS
speechtext:
The hon. member suggests that they won't wipe me out. They haven't wiped me out. Those boundaries carve up the city in a different way, that is all; it would probably be represented by this same member. But even if the commissioners have done things which some of us do not like, I still think this work should be carried out on an independent basis and that we should not snipe at them. I myself have had bitter experiences in two or three cases of redistribution by a committee of this House.
And now, having declared my faith, having said that I believe in the principle of redistribution by independent commissioners, I want to say a few words about the particular proposals in the bill presented to us this afternoon. The hon. member is asking that when the commissions make their reports to the House-reports which result in our having a chance to discuss them, though I am not sure about that; at least it is in the law-they should append explanations or justifications for the lines they have drawn. He says, and I think quite rightly, that this would make for better debate in the House. Indeed, it might in some cases do away with necessity for debate altogether.
My only concern, and I think it is probably met by the way the bill is drafted, is that the commissioners should
November 14, 1974

not be made responsible for producing unnecessary explanations. Out of 264 seats, or however many there may be, decisions in the cases of 200, or 225, are likely to be so obvious that no explanation would be required. But there will be occasions on which such drastic changes are made that hon. members will be justified in asking for an explanation. The way the bill is worded, or may be worded when it comes out of committee, can take care of that.
I hope, as I say, that the interpretation would be that in cases where an explanation is obviously called for, that explanation should be forthcoming, but that we would not put on the commissioners the responsibility of writing a long treatise in explanation of every constituency's boundaries in view of the fact that in many cases they would be quite understandable.
So, Mr. Speaker, let me stick to the unofficial agreement that we made about keeping speeches short and say that, with these comments on the part of one who firmly believes in redistribution by an independent commission, I am happy to see the bill before the House today, and I trust that it will go to committee not later than six o'clock.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING REASONS FOR COMMISSIONS' REPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will try not to exceed the ten minutes allowed to me, but first I would like to thank the member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) for having introduced that bill. He said a while ago that he was bringing it in for the third or fourth time. I suppose he believes in the saying: Practice makes perfect. This evening, he deserves our congratulations, because he prevented the government from killing his bill, since all members stated their views when the new legislation on the electoral boundaries readjustment was introduced. This legislation was not supported by all members. I think that the Electoral Boundaries Commission was blamed for its work.
A while ago I heard the member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) say that he would still prefer to entrust the work to an independent commission rather than to hon. members, even if it should indeed be assigned to them. If hon. members wish to give up that work and leave it to an independent organization, we will have to make sure, Mr. Speaker, that this commission acts with full knowledge of the facts.
Insofar as my area is concerned, I daresay I believed for a moment in this commission and I went along with the others in saying that we could give this work to an independent commission. But today, I am less of a dupe and I say that we need responsible people and the responsible people in this House are the Members of Parliament chosen by the people. When one has serious work to do it is not time to give it to others, it is time to take one's responsibilities.
When I finally got to know what the limits of Roberval riding were, I tried to discuss things with the commissioners and I was told it was too late, that everything had been done and that the act was about to become law. If a Member of Parliament does not have more authority than that in this House and if such an important matter as electoral limits is left up to a dictatorial organism, I
Electoral Boundaries
believe it is time for us to make a stand. We should not forget-and the commissioners seem to have done just that-that to trace the limits of a riding, it is not sufficient to take a piece of paper, to draw a line on it and say: "We are not going there". When a rural riding has a population of 50,000 to 60,000 with distances of 120 to 150 miles, this population is brought up to city levels, say 90,000, by taking two rural ridings and melting them into one; in the towns, it is easy, Mr. Speaker. Take four blocks and you get 90,000 or 95,000 population.
But in a rural area it is not the same thing and that is what I noticed when I examined the electoral act. I noticed that no account had been taken of the riding's demography or of the social or economic contacts of its population but these are essentials that cannot be ignored in a riding. For example, cutting up a small town of 10,000 or a parish in two and making the people go 150 miles on one side and those in the other part of the parish another 150 miles on the other side, just is not practical.
If we cannot find commissioners who are knowledgeable enough in their areas in each province and especially in Quebec to see that justice is done for the citizens of Quebec, I believe we will simply have to, not only improve the act, as proposed in Bill C-214, but repeal it and start all over again. If we can do otherwise, all the better. The government seems well disposed, but I for one was looking forward to December 31 with fear. I thought that, if the act was to be in force on December 31, and if no one did anything, it would have been a disaster, a revolution in my region. I have always thought the role of an MP was to serve his riding. At the present time, it would be physically impossible to serve a riding as big as that of Roberval that is to be created by the fusion of two ridings, those of Lac-Saint-Jean and Roberval. It is impossible and it took totally ignorant commissioners to propose such a thing.
I did not have the opportunity of appearing before the commission because I was not here at the time, but today I can say to the commissioners that they acted like dunces. If people cannot be found who are competent enough to do justice to the people, then let the job be entrusted to hon. members: they will do the job.
Of course, the Canadian population is growing. It is not absolutely necessary for Quebec to have 74 ridings. If the population increases, it is much easier, to my mind, to increase the number of ridings. Their number was increased in order to have all the Liberals on the same side. It would be much easier to increase the number of ridings, to do justice to the people, than to extend the limits of the ridings and thus make the members' task impossible to perform.
That, then, is what I wanted to say about the subject. I trust the bill will be sent to committee where it can be studied further. I am not a member of that committee, but I sincerely hope that its members will try to amend it; if need be, let them assume their responsibilities and present a bill that takes into account the needs of the people.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING REASONS FOR COMMISSIONS' REPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should first of all like to thank the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) for presenting this bill. I

November 14, 1974
Electoral Boundaries
might say I enjoyed the remarks of my neighbouring colleague, the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Blais), and was delighted that he also supports the bill. Certainly we both represent rural ridings, and along with a great many other members of parliament in this great country we want to see that rural areas are represented in the best way possible.
The previous bill before this House received a great deal of input from a great many of our sitting members of parliament who came out with the philosophy, "One man; one vote", and said this was how it was supposed to be. They asked why a rural elector should have a vote worth twice, or even more, that of a city elector? I am well aware of the great populations in our cities, especially those two great metropolitan areas, Montreal and Toronto. However, there are exceptions even in those areas where certain ridings comprise perhaps 20 by 30 city blocks containing a terrific number of electors. This, to a rural member, is absolutely crazy.
I can think of two ridings in metropolitan Toronto, I believe Spadina and Trinity, where there is a relatively small number of electors, much smaller than the number of actual residents. A great many people who reside in those ridings are not citizens and probably will not gain citizenship for some time, yet they are counted in the total population. Those members of parliament tell us to look at the number of people living in their ridings as compared to my riding of Parry Sound-Muskoka, for instance, which encompasses some 10,000 square miles with a population of 62,000 to 63,000 people, and an electorate of 43,000. This is one fact that ought to be drawn to our attention.
I should also like to congratulate the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), one of the sages of this House, who suggested that perhaps members of parliament cannot be entirely trusted to set boundaries, and for that reason an independent commission is much more appropriate.
There is some truth in that, but in a great many cases the members of parliament know a lot more about the boundaries and where they should be set than any independent commission. As I understand it, in the last drawing of boundaries some of the commissioners sat in their ivory towers in the cities of Toronto and Montreal Without ever going to the actual ridings. They were, therefore, not familiar with natural boundaries such as rivers, highways and so on. Certainly members of parliament might have a bias in respect of boundaries, but most of them are more knowledgeable as to proper location of boundaries than any independent commission.
I understand this bill is to receive approval on second reading and that there may be others who wish to speak, so I will not take any more time except to say that I support it, and I am pleased to see support for it from all sides of the House.
Before concluding I should mention that, as a result of the bill which is to come before the House next week or in the very near future, the province of Ontario will gain the greatest number of seats of any province-I believe seven to be exact. These seven additional seats will probably go to that golden horseshoe, the great metropolitan area of Toronto, and we in northern Ontario will again be left out, Mr. Speaker.

I want to point out to the hon. member for Nipissing that I class myself as part of that great northern part of the province, and we want to be damn sure that we are not going to be shortchanged or left out in the cold again as a result of that bill, while the great metropolitan area gets even more representation than that to which it is entitled. We know the population, of course, is in that area. I was again discouraged to hear the hon. member for Nipissing refer to the fact that over 90 per cent of the people living in Canada by the year 2000 will be living in that metropolitan area. That is not an encouraging fact for those of us who are living in the rural parts of Canada.
This again focuses attention on the fact that the British North America Act should perhaps be amended, throwing down the drain the 10 provinces and substituting five provinces, namely Montreal, Toronto, Vancouver, and I guess Winnipeg, with the other province being rural Canada. Let us hope that does not happen because rural people are entitled to the very best representation possible. Representation by population should not be the only criterion, any more than what some of us suggest, namely, representation by acreage.
Perhaps we should require a minimum of 5,000 square miles for each riding. If that were the case Toronto and Montreal would come out on the dirty end of the stick, but there has to be some reasoning in order that rural areas of Canada are protected. If independent commissions are to set these boundaries for redistribution, that is fine, but I think they should have some guidance from members of parliament.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING REASONS FOR COMMISSIONS' REPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to confirm what the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling) has said, that there will shortly be introduced in the House a bill to amend the British North America Act. However, that bill will only deal with redistribution of parliamentary seats as between provinces, and will not deal with redistribution of seats within provinces. It will provide for a modest increase in the size of this House, and I can assure hon. members that I am not telling tales out of school because those members who were active on the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections during the last parliament are aware of these details.
Let me now make a few remarks about the bill before us, put forward in the name of the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert). One of the things frustrating all members is that, when looking at previous maps, we find that proposed redistribution will not only affect us individually and personally but will also affect the constituents in our ridings.
We are frustrated when trying to discover any logical and coherent philosophy behind the decisions of the provincial commissions. To compound that confusion, very often there is no continuation of any common philosophy on the part of the commissioners as between provinces. In other words, we find 10 different philosophies in respect of redistribution within a province. I do not deny, because of the way the population is spread out through our country, that this is desirable. However, I do feel that this bill provides a correction to the kind of laissez-faire attitude commissions take in determining how redistribution is to take place.
November 14, 1974

Those who have the responsibility for taking a decision it seems to me should also have the responsibility to provide reasons for having taken that decision. Right now the commissions are in the position of being able to take a decision without having to give any reason. I cannot think of anything more irresponsible. However, the legislation permits that, and this amendment would have the effect of forcing the commissions to make a reasoned argument to justify what they are doing in a province. It may have a much more substantial effect in respect of the way in which redistribution takes place within a province than is now the case.
I feel the principle of having to explain the reason for a decision is a good one, not only in respect of redistribution but in respect of other spheres of activity. Therefore I am happy to support this bill. I am pleased that it will go to the Committee on Privileges and Elections.
I would hope that when the bill goes to committee we would have an opportunity to focus attention on the principle in the redistribution bill concerning the distribution of seats within a province.
My last comment is to remind hon. members that this bill is no solution to the problem of distribution of seats within a province. It does not touch on that. I do not think it is right for members to raise expectations where there are no expectations possible. It is a very limited bill. I think it will have a very desirable effect. It is a desirable amendment, and I am delighted to support it.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE ADMINISTRATION OF INTERPROVINCIAL, EXPORT AND IMPORT TRADE IN PETROLEUM AND PETROLEUM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at five o'clock I was responding to a number of points which had been put to me by the hon. member for Crowfoot who was with us at that time. I dealt with his query about oil pricing and said that of course the major international companies, such as Imperial Oil and Gulf, would like the price to go up to the international price as soon as possible, but that this government does not happen to agree with that and we think we have the means to protect the Canadian consumer.
The same is true with regard to natural gas. While we think that over a period of time it would be desirable to move to a commodity value relationship between oil and natural gas, we do not think that this should occur in one year. There have been some suggestions by members, such as the hon. member for Crowfoot, that this would be of exclusive benefit to central Canada, as though there was something wrong with that particular group of Canadians being protected in this way.
With regard to natural gas perhaps I can remind the House, and members from Saskatchewan and Manitoba in particular, that they too are the consumers of Alberta natural gas, indeed that a far greater percentage per capita of individual householders in those two provinces than of householders in Ontario and Quebec use natural gas. They as consumers would also be grievously affected if the price of gas were allowed to go to commodity value at this point.
It is for that reason that the government has proposed a formula for phasing up the price of gas, over a period of years, to commodity value in a way that would be fair to the producing provinces, but at the same time softening the impact on the individual consumer.
One of the questions which the hon. member raised was with regard to the financing of the Montreal pipeline. He said that the government should give an undertaking to the company in question which, as he pointed out, was a subsidiary of a number of major international oil companies, in order to make certain that the pipeline would be built.
The position which the government has been taking is that the public purse should not be exposed to any more expenditure for building this pipeline than absolutely necessary to make certain that it goes through. In other words, in certain circumstances we could indeed give some

November 14, 1974
Oil and Petroleum
very expensive undertakings to the company. We think, however-and this has been the tenor of our negotiations-that we should achieve our objectives without exposing the taxpayer to a substantial potential expenditure in the future if the contingency about which the company is concerned should in fact take place.
The hon. member for Crowfoot raised a question about the number of amendments which I have distributed to other parties on behalf of the government, and which we intend to put to the House in due course. As I said when I introduced this stage of the proceedings yesterday, there have indeed been a number of amendments worked out by my advisers as a result of representations made following scrutiny of the bill by the general public. I make no apology for that. It seems to me that that is exactly what the three readings procedure of our House of Commons is about, that the bill should be given first reading and that members of the public who will be affected by it, who may be in special situations which may be adversely affected by the application of any clause of the bill, should have the opportunity to respond. The government should take account of this kind of response and, in due course, put forward amendments. That seems to me to be a reasonable and sensible course of action, far more sensible than saying, "We put the bill down, it is graven in stone and we will make no changes."
Finally the hon. member for Crowfoot asked what would be the formula for the pricing of petroleum after June 30, 1975. I think that probably the best answer is the answer that was given by the ten provincial premiers and the Prime Minister when they met a week or so ago in connection with inflation, that is, that the appropriate oil price after the end of the agreement which they negotiated on March 27 should be a matter of further discussion and negotiation in May, 1975.
I think that at that time there will obviously be some conflicting views coming in, on the one hand from the producing provinces saying, "Let us go to the highest possible international price right now so that we can get the full benefit," and on the other hand from the consumers, namely, British Columbia and the provinces to the east of Saskatchewan, saying "Come now, let us keep the price down so that we do not have to absorb this in a short period of time." This will be a matter of negotiation between the premiers of the different regions under the leadership of the Prime Minister.
The hon. member has been saying that we should conduct this kind of negotiation rather than adopt, by fiat, and in advance, the kind of formula which it is suggested will be followed. I think I have responded to the questions raised by the hon. gentleman and will be glad to clarify further, if I can.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE ADMINISTRATION OF INTERPROVINCIAL, EXPORT AND IMPORT TRADE IN PETROLEUM AND PETROLEUM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have a further question to put to the minister and I should like something clarified. First, let me comment on something the minister suggested before supper. No member on this side of the House believes, so far as I know, that Canadians should suffer because of fluctuating oil prices, or because of high prices charged on the wprld markets for oil. We want to see stable oil prices and a mechanism in this country which

will keep them stable. Further, we want to make sure that oil exploration in Canada is not discouraged.
Before supper the minister was somewhat political in his remarks. The trained seals behind him thumped their desks at the suggestion that the Liberal party stands for cheap oil for central and eastern Canada and the Conservative party for world oil prices for all Canadians. This House must meet any such suggestion head on. We must assure Canadians in all parts of Canada that we are all in favour of continued energy supplies, and that no Canadian will be asked to go short of energy today in return for some possible benefit in the future. The minister has suggested that there must be a trade-off between our needs of today and those of tomorrow. I do not think any Canadian has ever agreed to such a bargain. We suggest that the price should be high enough to encourage continued exploration in Canada.
The minister said that the $6.50 per barrel price will prevail until July 1, 1975, after which he, or the commission to be established under the bill, may renegotiate the price. That brings me to my point. Why are we dealing with this bill today? Why has it been given such high priority, in view of the imminence of the budget which is to be presented on November 18? The previous budget of May created great uncertainty in the oil and gas industry, as it proposed that royalties paid to provinces should not be considered as an expense. Yet here we are discussing a bill to do with energy, a bill which will confer certain powers on the commission to be set up, and we do not know what the next budget will propose.
The people in the oil and gas industry are uncertain. The minister has been in western Canada and talked to the people of Calgary who, I am sure, were not bashful in presenting their views. He knows the extent to which the coming budget will affect employment and exploration activities. The companies are waiting. They have made out their expenditure programs, but want to see what the budget will propose. The minister did not touch on that topic at all.
To show how ridiculous this debate is, let me quote from a transcript of an interview which the Prime Minister gave Ron Robert on November 13, 1974. Mr. Robert was discussing the Mackenzie Valley pipeline. I will not read the question, but the Prime Minister said this, in answer to whether the pipeline would be built:
No, this is a policy which has been discussed in caucus. I don't think that the caucus has been divided on it, I mean in terms of regions. There are individuals of course who feel strongly against the Mackenzie pipeline, and those who feel very strongly in favour of it. You know the government's position on it.
Now comes the key phrase:
It is one of waiting for the National Energy Board to state, well, the facts of the situation:-
The point is that we are being asked to pass this legislation tonight, but the Prime Minister said that the government policy is one of waiting for the National Energy Board to report. I continue quoting:
-how much energy do we have, how much it will cost, and so on. It's only after that that the government will have to give precise answers as to timing and financing and so on, and at that point, caucus will be involved. They can give their opinions too when they've seen the National Energy Board report.
November 14, 1974

The Prime Minister wants his caucus to read the report from the National Energy Board, but he wants this House to pass this particular piece of legislation at this time. He does not want this House to exercise the judgment which his caucus will be asked to exercise. How foolish can one be. Before supper the minister suggested that the National Energy Board report to the government, that the report will not necessarily be made available to parliament, but that out of the graciousness of his good heart he will let the two producing provinces, Saskatchewan and Alberta, see it. At no time did he suggest that the report will ever be made public, not even after it has been printed in French and in English!
Actually he hinted it may never be made public. Such failure to disclose would be a sin against the Canadian voter. What did the Prime Minister say? He is the guiding light in this country and he knows how important is the report of the National Energy Board. He said that the government's position is "... one of waiting for the National Energy Board to state, well, the facts of the situation." Only then will the government give precise answers as to timing, financing and so on, and at that point caucus will be involved. According to the Prime Minister, "They can give their opinions, too, when they've seen the National Energy Board report."
Although I have not consulted my colleagues, I think I speak for them when I say that it would be proper for someone to rise and move the adjournment of this debate, and ask the House to deal with other legislation. Surely we are entitled to the same privileges extended to the Liberal caucus. Surely we should be asked for our opinion after we, too, have read the National Energy Board report. Asking us to pass this bill now is an insult to our intelligence and an insult to the intelligence of parliament, especially in view of what the Prime Minister said on November 13.

tion of what the Prime Minister does by insisting on knowing all the facts. How can constructive criticism be expected from the opposition until we have all the facts from the National Energy Board report?

speechtext: Thank you very much.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE ADMINISTRATION OF INTERPROVINCIAL, EXPORT AND IMPORT TRADE IN PETROLEUM AND PETROLEUM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Will the minister state that those facts will be given to the public before November 18 so that we will know the impact of the budget on the production capabilities of our industry for the betterment of all Canadians? That is the question.
All or most exploration companies, both Canadian and international, are waiting for the budget. The report of the National Energy Board should be in their hands and our hands before the budget comes down so that we can appraise the exact attitude of the government with regard to further exploration.
As I said before the dinner hour, this is the only country in the world that has turned down exploration for the past two years. Was it foolishness, extravagance or do we really have that much that we can turn off exploration? I think the National Energy Board report will make it abundantly clear that we were in fact foolish to turn off exploration. We have lost a time gap which was ours. We could have caught up and met our needs after 1983. Regardless of whether Petro Canada pours millions of dollars into the tar sands, we will still be in a deficit position until after 1983 when production from the tar sands should catch up with our demand. Also, we must uncover more resources than are now known in both the oil and gas fields.
Will the National Energy Board report be made public to members of this House and the industry, or will it be kept solely for the purpose of the Liberal Party? Will it be made public prior to the evening of November 18? I will give the minister an extra half day and only ask for it prior to that evening.
It is of vital importance to the industry and all Canadians to know where they are going. If the minister really wants to serve Canada, he will stand in his place and ask that this debate now cease. The House Leader can bring in other pieces of legislation. We could deal with some of the Senate bills that are before the House if the government wants to kill an extra hour and a half tonight.
Let us treat parliament with some degree of respect. The minister should show the same amount of respect that the Prime Minister is prepared to show the Liberal caucus.

Mr. Chairman, I think the basic theme of the hon. member's remarks were in his last few words when he talked about killing the remaining hour and a half this evening. There is an important point that should be made for the record. The Leader of the Opposition is making threats about continuing the debate. That is fine. I hope the record will note that.
I am sure the hon. member for Crowfoot would not want to mislead this House or the readers of Hansard in what he said. The National Energy Board report that Mr. Robert

November 14, 1974
Oil and Petroleum
referred to in his question was not the report about which the hon. member questioned me yesterday. The report he was referring to was the one with regard to the Mackenzie Valley Pipeline which will be produced by that board after a full set of hearings for which application is now being made before the board.
I am sure the hon. member would not try to mislead the House by taking quotations out of context. With regard to the National Energy Board report on oil, I responded to the hon. member on this question as reported at page 1286 of yesterday's Hansard. I indicated it had been put in the hands of the provincial government. It has not yet been put in the hands of my colleagues, either of cabinet or caucus. It will, of course, be made public as soon as we are in a position, as I indicated before supper, to announce our intention with regard to the appropriate export level.
It is important to get the reaction of the government of Alberta on this. It will be of serious importance to the level of production in that province. I agree it would certainly be of assistance if we had it at this point, but unfortunately we do not. The government will wait with patience for the provinces. If in due course they are not prepared to respond, we will have to take our responsibility.
I am sure parliament will want to react to it. I hope members will react intelligently. What the government will do is make its decision as to the proper level of exports, taking into account whatever level of exports the province of Alberta may think appropriate. We will take our responsibility in this regard.
I look forward to any meaningful substantive response which the Leader of the Opposition or his colleagues may have in this regard. I will welcome it. When it gets down to the substance of dealing with this energy question, I think I can say that the Leader of the Opposition has been almost the least informative man in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is my first opportunity to speak in this debate. I would say that the minister's true colours are now coming out. As far as the oil and gas business are concerned, prior to September, 1973, I thought that all he knew was that gasoline came out of a pump and oil was brought to your home by a truck. I thought that was all he knew about production and the background of the industry.
On Labour Day 1973, this government imposed the export tax. That was the beginning of the intervention by this government. If there ever has been an industry in this country that has suffered from ham-handed amateurs not only tinkering but slamming with sledgehammers, it is the oil industry.
Hon. members think the oil industry is something that exists way out somewhere. They do not bother with it. I say to hon. members that businesses in their constituencies later this year and next year will have cancelled orders for unfilled sales because the supply firms that deal with the oil industry have to cut back.
We must look at the number of drill rigs that have left. We must look at the capital that has been committed elsewhere by the oil companies. Over 60 per cent of the

wells drilled in this country are drilled by independents, but because of the action of the government, the tax proposals of last May and the attempted long range control of the industry, Canadian companies are unable to raise capital and have been forced to cease operations with the result that Canadians are being laid off. If the government only knew the damage it was causing to Canadian industry! But that is beyond its ken.
We know there was a meeting in January, but that was a preliminary meeting. Neither the government of Canada nor the premiers of the provinces knew much about what they were discussing at that time. Mr. Chairman, I wish to make just a few general comments on Bill C-32, which is to become the national petroleum administration act. At the outset let me say that I am a strong nationalist and that the welfare of all Canadians must be our first concern. I believe that we as Albertans, because of our past actions, have shown this to be the case. But what disturbs me is that the federal government now wishes to fleece the western region of our country. This bill will seriously undercut Alberta's constitutional authority. I say this not only as a concerned Albertan but as a concerned Canadian. If the federal government is allowed to invade provincial authority in this area, what is going to stop it from invading provincial authority in other areas? Other provinces have other resources that may well be on the chopping block of this federal administration.
Throughout history natural resources have been a lot more than mere financial problems of provincial and federal governments. It now appears that the federal government wants all the gravy. For 50 years the west lived or died on its agricultural base. Now the oil fields and gas fields have changed that considerably. A great many of the benefits that have emerged in the west over recent years are the result of our natural resource development, and the same is true for the future. It is not only a matter of money, but the principle of Ottawa's interfering where it ought not to be interfering. Ottawa is intruding simply because it wishes to have part of the bonanza, only because it wishes to have part of this wealth.
Ottawa's interference is going to stagnate our oil development. Rising world prices should be serving to stimulate the exploration of oil development, but this will not happen with the system that the federal government plans to impose. This government has responded with great enthusiasm, hiring more people to survey, to collect data, and to search for reasons as to why it should be involved in this area. As far as I am concerned, the government has created more problems that it has cured. The more government becomes involved, the more it is going to cost us. If it takes 20 per cent of the wage earner's money now, it will

November 14, 1974
Oil and Petroleum
take 30 to 50 per cent after the government has taken control.
It is hard for me to understand why so many people want more government involvement. In Manitoba there is a government that wishes to control everything, yet one of its own corporations, Manitoba Hydro, is contracting out more of its work to private individuals because it gets no efficiency out of its own departments.
The federal government is putting artificial props in certain places and plugging certain holes at different times, and the result is total confusion. Now is the time to stop this confusion and to formulate policies so that one area is not discriminated against in the way that this bill provides. We, as elected representatives, have a responsibility to guard against these interferences, and now is the time for us to act. Bill C-32 is an intrusion on provincial authority, and for that reason I do not believe it is worthy of our support.

Mr. Chairman, this debate now going on on Bill C-32 is rather important, I would say very important, since it concerns federal-provincial relations on energy development and use.
The development as well as the use of energy have until now been matters of provincial jurisdiction and reasonably accepted as such.
However, because there have been for a couple of years restrictions or an alleged shortage of energy, the federal government took the initiative in poking its nose in provincial matters. It has not been doing so for only two years!
I remember very well, as do my colleagues who then sat in the House, the ferocious battle the government of British Columbia had to fight against the federal government with regard to the agreements British Columbia and the United States had concluded about the Columbia River Treaty.
Ottawa thrust its nose into that to embarrass the provincial government and, in the end, the provincial authorities were fairly victorious. No Canadian province wants the federal government to interfere in its affairs. Be it Alberta, British Columbia, Quebec, the Maritimes, each one cherishes its autonomy and refuses to be dictated to by Ottawa.
This, Mr. Chairman, does not prevent meetings between Canadian provinces and the federal government, in the mutual respect of the two levels of government, but with constant consideration for the provincial rights so that they may not be infringed upon and so that the provinces may take their own decisions. I think that there is no Canadian in Alberta who would want the Maritimes to suffer and that there is none in the Maritimes who would wish such a fate for the western provinces. This is my conviction. That there should be elements protesting against one another, elements from the west against those from the east or from the east against the west, this is obviously inevitable. These people hinder not only the development of our natural resources, but the spirit of

Canadian unity because they are taking completely foolish positions.
Recently, I had occasion to meet, in Toronto, on Pierre Berton's program, Mr. Harridence, a separatist lawyer from Alberta. He lives in Calgary. I believe he was at one time either leader of the Conservative party in Alberta or a candidate to the leadership of that party. He is the fellow who said, out west, during the pseudo energy crisis: "Let those eastern bastards freeze in the dark." A separatist-

That reflected the same spirit that animates some people we hear in the east who say: "If things are not going well in Canada, it is because the west spends its time begging for help. The west gets more than the east." Some even make of it a French versus the English problem.
In the meantime, all hell breaks loose; hardly any problems are solved and the federal government, instead of putting out the fires, instead of setting up a consultation system, throws oil on the fire, compounding the problem. So, this is where we are now, Mr. Chairman, and I think the federal government should play a leading part and assume its own responsibilities, not by restricting provincial rights but by gathering the provinces at a round table and having them agree to let all Canadians benefit from our natural resources. Then, Mr. Chairman, I think Canadians would be satisfied.
Anyone today can say: We have oil out west, so who cares about the others. But who can tell that in five or ten years oil will still be in as great demand as it is today? Will nuclear energy not be used for pacific purposes, or will it not replace oil just as oil supplanted coal? The federal government then has to interfere with coal mining activities, not only in the maritime provinces, but also in the western provinces, to help them develop those natural resources. But that is no reason why the federal government should say: Those riches belong to us because no province wants to share what it has got.
In Quebec, the magic word is hydroelectric power, and that is natural, we have more than enough-and then some. Same thing as regards forests. Sometimes, a province may own riches required by the whole population, then later it has to turn to another province to get another commodity. So why should we say: We are going to tax Alberta because its products are selling so well at the moment. Its products are in such demand that we are going to tax it to punish it for having too many natural resources. And the same attitude would apply to Quebec and Ontario. Why should we say that?
In the mining field for instance, some mining companies are now urging the federal government to let them go ahead with the development of new mines. That is as far as it goes because the government would immediately be told: you take from us our gains, our profits. So, the companies are not interested in working for the benefit of the government.
Same situation in Alberta, where nobody is interested in working for the benefit of the government. Saskatchewan
November 14, 1974

owns other natural resources, potash for example. Is Saskatchewan willing to have its policy dictated by the federal government? No.
The federal government's role is to maintain balance and harmony among all the provinces, and the only way to do so is to respect the authority and autonomy of every one of them. I believe the federal government should act as a conciliator, but also as the agent which will examine the possibilities for Canadians to benefit from the development of those natural resources on the international markets.
Mr. Chairman, there is not one provincial premier in Canada who wants to kneel before the federal government to get the permission to exploit the resources of his province. The former premier of Saskatchewan-he is sitting on my right-did not want Ottawa to dictate what he was to do. He had to take his responsibilities, he wanted to take them. The same thing is valid today for the other provincial premiers.
I, for one, say that Ottawa should not penalize a province because it has natural resources, but it should help that province get the maximum out of its natural resources and always keep in mind first, the fulfillment of the needs of the Canadian people, and then consider exports, if we have something left to trade with others. Exports should not be taxed in one province to punish it because it is exporting oil to the United States, for example. Quebec should not be penalized for exporting electricity to Ontario or to the United States; that would be absolutely ridiculous.
Bill C-32 would allow us to tax provinces with production surpluses or natural resources. Mr. Chairman, that bill will not last ten years before some government, whoever they might be, will regret it and will probably have to, if not cancel it, at least amend it to allow the provinces to get on with their own business and be shown the respect they deserve.

Mr. Chairman, this debate has been good in that it has drawn attention to certain factors that have been overlooked. The main question is whether the government's stand on the price of oil will assure us of a supply in the next four, five or 10 years. Canada has an abundance of energy resource for the foreseeable future, but it will be expensive, and we are now being warned by industry that we could well have a shortage in the early 1980's. Even taking into allowance industrial over-statement, I think we might well have a shortage of conventional crude in the 1980's and become more dependent on foreign supplies.
I think we face this possible future shortage because of the rigidity in setting the price at $6.50 without encouraging development. We are assuming that because $6.50 is high, companies will still continue to search for oil, when in fact oil companies feel they might as well cease exploration and take whatever they can get now, then when the oil runs out they will not have lost anything. I think we are making a grave mistake because we are now at the stage the United States oil industry found itself in the early 1950's. At that time the price of oil and gas was such that it encouraged wasteful use rather than conservation.
Oil and Petroleum
That wasteful use is now taking place here, and I cite, for example, the use of natural gas to fire some of Ontario Hydro's generating plants.
I do not think that this pricing mechanism of the government will encourage the supply of oil and gas. Coupled with this price the government has set of $6.50, and no indication of what will be done to encourage production and exploration, we have had the budget of last spring which was termed a disaster so far as the oil industry was concerned. Certainly until the twin problem of setting a proper price for oil and the mechanism for doing it is devised-until we know what the government intends to do so far as this is concerned-we really will not have any meaningful discussion of the problem.
Obviously the oil industry can only continue exploration if it is allowed a fair return on its investment. It is stated that the cash flow in respect of new oil would be $1.66 in Alberta on the basis of the May budget proposals, whereas in the United States for new oil the cash flow would be about $5.06 after allowing royalties of 12.5 per cent and a corporate tax of 48 per cent. Exploration is more attractive in the United States.
Apparently some 40 companies have opened offices in Denver, Colorado, and 10 per cent of Canadian drilling rigs are down there. Until we at least reach a normal level of exploration it would seem that we face considerable difficulty. It has been forecast that out of 250 drilling rigs which have been available in Alberta and British Columbia only 110 will be available in these two provinces by next January. This means that we are losing these rigs-the minister has not denied this-and are also losing experienced personnel. This is an indication that in Canada we cannot isolate ourselves from the United States or world markets.
What is the problem in respect of the $6.50 per barrel price? The system is rigid. There is no premium for new oil. There is no differential between old oil, adolescent oil or new oil, and with the present tax situation the industry does now know where it is headed.
As I have said, I suggest there is too much rigidity in respect of the pricing of oil by the government. I would hope that by his attitude the minister would show that he hopes to have some sort of a differential for new oil flows. There must be a standard method of encouraging production. If this were the situation the bill might be seen in a better light. But certainly the pricing of oil as set forth in this bill would indicate that the exploration and production of oil are secondary to holding down the price. While this might be advantageous to all of us, because we like to have low priced oil, it will not do us much good if the result should be a shortage in four or five years.

Little did I know. I will have to find that teacher and tell him that he has not met Donald Macdonald.
There is one point that I would like to make regarding gas price controls, a subject which has not been discussed to any great degree. The minister indicated that he feels it will be necessary to control gas prices up to commodity

value. I hope that everybody heard him say "up to commodity value" because, based on past experience, we can expect some pronouncements in the not too distant future regarding the meaning of commodity value, a meaning which might be totally remote from any realistic meaning. Although it may not do any good, let me remind the minister that that would be another broken commitment.
I think it is worth mentioning that the price of natural gas in Canada has never been at commodity level. It has always been underpriced. Tragically this has resulted in waste, and this is probably the best view fit. In terms of its potential for producing fertilizers, chemicals and other higher value added commodities, it is a tragedy to be wasting this fuel in generating electricity and in other ways.
It is certainly high time that we brought this valuable fuel up to commodity value so that this wastage can cease. I think it bears mentioning-although that probably will not have any influence on the government-that the only thing that is preventing natural gas from seeking its fair value, its commodity value on the market, is the fact that we have a monopoly purchasing situation. You can remove that monopoly, that bottleneck, from the entire market if you require TransCanada Pipe Lines to be a common carrier. If you take that simple action the market place will establish the true and fair level of gas prices. We do not need a hired bunch of experts. Mr. Chairman, I have been sitting in this House now for a few hours listening to this debate. I am going to make a few brief remarks and then ask a simple question, to which, I frankly doubt, I will get a simple answer. As my colleagues have discovered, there do not seem to be any answers forthcoming. I am not going to duplicate many of the points the Leader of the Opposition made far better than I could regarding the constitutional difficulties concerning this particular piece of legislation.
As a member from Ontario I have asked questions in the House and expressed concern regarding transportation in my province. I have pointed out on different occasions errors that have been made to the tune of hundreds of
November 14, 1974

millions of dollars in the public works estimates, and I have asked questions about unemployment insurance involving expenditure of almost $1 billion. However, last winter many of my constituents, including myself, began to become concerned about a shortage of fuel. At that time we were told, after talking to some of our colleagues from Alberta as well as provincial officials, that they are Canadians first and that, as far as they were able, they were not going to see Canada short of energy.
It then became obvious that to fulfil this promise a pipe line was necessary. It was also obvious that the pipe line which, for want of a better word, had been imposed upon this country by the right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert a few years previously was indeed one of the smartest moves this country had ever seen.
It is a fact, of course, that we in Ontario have for a number of years been paying a premium on our oil. That is fair enough; we have paid premiums before. Then we started hearing talk about this pipe line which was necessary to carry oil further east, and we also heard some nonsense about having a two-way pipe line. Now, Mr. Chairman, any huckleberry from Ontario knows that you cannot suck and blow at the same time; it does not take much expertise to find that out. So we are concerned anew with the energy situation.
We are now faced with Bill C-32. Despite the government's obvious dislike for price fixing or price controls, and with the government's heavy accentuation on combines legislation, we now find out that a price is going to be forced on the province of Alberta if negotiations do not meet with success. We do not know what the price is, but a price will be forced upon that province.
It seems to me that this is a particularly large club. If that club were being used against the province of Ontario in connection with its nickel, or its uranium, or other products of a similar nature, the minister would have a bigger fight on his hands than he has right now.
I listened to the speech of the hon. member for Crowfoot. I think it is fair to say that one thing that the hon. member for Crowfoot and I have in common is that we rarely agree on things. But I think that anyone who misjudges his intelligence on a subject like this, and that of his many colleagues, makes a very real mistake.
I must admit that the longer I sit here the more concerned I become. Indeed, I am also a little confused. My colleagues from Alberta used terminology and referred to quantities that are a wee bit beyond my ken, perhaps; but the single thought comes through that there is something wrong with this legislation. There is something here that does not sit well with Canadians, and I remind the committee that these members from Alberta are Canadians.
To take this a step further, during the question period my next door neighbour and the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings often ask questions about the level of production in Canada compared with the level of production throughout the world, and the fact that Canada's balance of payments is getting into a bit of trouble. If there is less exploration of our resources and we are not able to export some of our products, what is going to happen to our balance of payments? Where will we get the

money to pay the tariff on incoming oil, so as to guarantee a single price, if we do not export?
I am sure that the calm, reasoned and logical approach of the Leader of the Opposition, when put up against the hon. "flim-flam" man from Toronto and some of the things he said this evening, is going to appeal to the people of Canada. Certainly I have not heard the minister give us any answers this evening.

CONSUMER AFFAIRS-INCREASE IN PRICE OF PERSONAL HEALTH CARE PRODUCTS-SUGGESTED INVESTIGATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in following up questions I asked the then minister of consumer and corporate affairs in the last session of parliament I asked the present minister on November 5 whether he has directed an investigation under the Combines Investigation Act into the unwarranted increases in the cost of personal health care products.
It is my contention that the ripoff cliche could not be better applied to unwarranted profits than in the field of most personal health care products. It is obvious that despite all the time and investigation by responsible authorities we cannot seem to find solutions to control the cost of food, but certainly there are many commodities used in the home which are increasing in price almost as

November 14, 1974
Adjournment Debate
fast as foods, along with clothing and housing. I refer particularly to costs of personal health care products which take up a goodly portion of the family budget, and which could be controlled by responsible and reasonable government legislation.
Surely we can see just how much money is being wasted by housewives as a result of advertising hucksterism used by advertising agencies and most cosmetic firms. Surely we could show the consumers the waste, and thereby save them many millions of dollars in their budgets, which would leave them more dollars to acquire the essential foods they need for their families.
Not only are the consumers the victims of cosmetic hucksterism, being ripped off, they are using products which might even be injurious to their health, or which are indeed of little or no use.
I was pleased to note that after the many references I have made to the subject over the past two or three years, but to no avail, the CTV program "Inquiry" exposed the matter recently on television, for which it should be commended. It revealed the phoniness which exists because of artificial freedom of enterprise.
Apart from the fact that the television program revealed that some half a billion dollars is being spent for personal care products, and most of that money is being wasted as a result of saturation advertising, and that a product costing a few cents can be sold for many dollars, depending on the name and the advertising clout of the firm promoting the product, this situation still exists.
I took it upon myself last year to purchase two cans of hairspray, one at a cost of 98 cents and another at a cost of about $3. I sent them to the Food and Drug Directorate for analysis, and I should like to read you the results in part:
The limited analysis available so far suggests that the majority of the spray (97 to 99 per cent) is made up of propellants and solvents ... with other lubricating, perfuming, and coating agents making up the balance. The products are similar in composition, though the amounts of individual ingredients will naturally vary somewhat.
The details could not be provided because it was given on a confidential basis for branch use only.
A similar situation exists, I am sure, in respect of most other cosmetic products, and I mention anti-perspirants, hairdressings, nail polishes, lipsticks, mascara, creams and lotions. In this regard I would refer you to the "Consumer Contact" report of September, 1974, and I quote:
Cosmetics in Canada are required by federal law, under The Food and Drugs Act, to be free of injurious substances, to be packaged in safe and non-deceptive containers and produced under sanitary conditions.
Later in the same report it states:
Rare or precious ingredients are seldom, if ever, included in cosmetic formulas and there is no need to pay a high price to obtain an effective product for any cosmetic use.
For example, the report states:
Deodorants are designed to eliminate the odour of perspiration without checking its flow. Use of mild soap and water has always been effective. Prolonged and repeated use of aerosol underarm deodorants, if they are inhaled, may have adverse effects in the lungs, while feminine hygiene sprays may cause some local irritation.

The report further states:
The skin is nourished by normal food consumption and not by externally applied creams, lotions, or other substances.
Hair cannot be restored to bald heads by application of salves, ointments, and other preparations applied externally, nor by shampoos, manipulation and various mechanical devices.
In another area the report states:
Dandruff is readily removed by washing the hair and scalp with any good shampoo. Indiscriminate use of medicated products may result in severe skin reactions.
Reduction of excess weight can be achieved safely and effectively only by a proper diet, a decrease in the amount of food eaten, and to some extent, by a good deal of exercise. There are no solutions, preparations, or devices applied externally, or pills taken internally that can truthfully claim to have a slimming effect without an accompanying reduction of food intake on a low calorie diet.
Lipstick of the long-lasting indelible type is a frequent cause of irritation. There are, however, a number of lipsticks that do not contain the bromoacid dyes which are usually the chief offenders. Look for what are called 'Hypo-allergenic' brands.
Organic or 'natural' cosmetics have become quite fashionable, but they have no special values.
The most common sources of allergic problems are perfumes, antiperspirants and deodorants, dyes, chemical depilatories, nail lacquer and other nail preparations, indelible lipsticks and sunscreen preparations.
Good looks are derived from good health. Cultivate it by eating wisely, keeping regular hours, avoiding excess use of liquor, soft drinks, and other sweets.

subtopic: CONSUMER AFFAIRS-INCREASE IN PRICE OF PERSONAL HEALTH CARE PRODUCTS-SUGGESTED INVESTIGATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has raised a number of points in his remarks tonight. He referred to such things as possible misleading advertising. If that is in fact the case and he has evidence, the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs would be interested in obtaining such evidence so that it would be able to take appropriate action.
Further, there has been mention made of possible health hazards in respect of such products as cosmetics and other things to which the hon. member referred. This is not part of the responsibility of our department, but I am sure the Department of National Health and Welfare would be very interested in any evidence the hon. member may have in respect of real health hazards for Canadians.
The hon. member referred to an information program which appeared last weekend on CTV in respect of cosmetics and their usefulness or lack of it. I think that kind of approach is very worthwhile in terms of informing the Canadian people as to the merits or demerits of products or lines of products in the cosmetic field.
I would compliment the CTV and others who provide this kind of public information to the people of Canada. I must admit I do not really have the view that the people of Canada are so naive as not to be able to recognize the quality of many of these products but because of simple cosmetic vanity are inclined to use them.
The hon. member asked whether the minister was proceeding with an investigation under the Combines Investigation Act. As the hon. member realizes, such investigation must be carried on on a confidential basis. Therefore the minister is not in a position either to confirm or deny
November 14, 1974

that such an investigation is taking place. However, if the hon. member, or any other hon. member or members of the public generally, feel that there is justification for charges to be laid under the Combines Investigation Act, they can rest assured that the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs will take appropriate action on the basis of any valid evidence submitted.

subtopic: CONSUMER AFFAIRS-PRICE OF ANTI-FREEZE-REASON FOR INCREASED MARKUP AND POSSIBILITY OF PROFITEERING
CONSUMER AFFAIRS-PRICE OF ANTI-FREEZE-REASON FOR INCREASED MARKUP AND POSSIBILITY OF PROFITEERING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 13 I asked the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) whether he found any evidence of profiteering in the anti-freeze industry in Canada, and his reply was no. I wonder how the minister can be so complacent in the light of the present situation.
Today anti-freeze is selling at 100 per cent more than a year ago, and in some cases even higher than that. In 1973 a consumer could buy a gallon of anti-freeze for $2.40. In 1974 prices range between $6.88 a gallon and $12 a gallon. Indeed, in my constituency of Sault Ste. Marie at the retail level the price of anti-freeze varies from distributor to distributor. At Canadian Tire the price is $6.88 a gallon; at Western Tire, it is $7.98; at Esso, $8.00; at Fina, $8.95; at Gulf, $9; at Texaco, $9.50, at Supertest, $9.95; at Sunoco, $10; at Shell, $10.95; There are variations among service station operators, some charging as high as $12 a gallon.
What, I ask, are retailers paying to the wholesalers for their supplies? Figures I have obtained from a co-operative store in Oshawa indicate the following: in 1972 the retailer purchased anti-freeze from the distributor at an average price of $2.25 a gallon; in 1973, the average price was $2.65 a gallon; but in 1974 the price varies from $6.15 a gallon to $9.75 a gallon that the corner gas station must pay to the wholesaler.
Why is there this tremendous mark-up? The minister says it is because the cost of the raw material, ethylene glycol, has gone up due to shortages. True, the cost has gone up somewhat, and we should try to determine whether they are real shortages or not, sufficient to justify anti-freeze selling at $9 to $12. In 1972 ethylene glycol was imported at 73 cents a gallon; in 1973 it was imported at $1.08 a gallon and in 1974 at $3.35 a gallon. I have found out that in 1972 the mark-up was roughly $1.50 a gallon over the import price, but today the mark-up is from $4 to $6 over the import price.
How does the minister justify a $6 mark-up over the basic import price of ethylene glycol? He cannot. The evidence is that the middleman and the manufacturer have conspired to raise prices unjustfiably. I charge that the Canadian manufacturers of anti-freeze have deliberately avoided increasing their production capacity at a time of rising demand, thereby creating an artificial scarcity of ethylene. Coupled with this, they spread rumours of a scarcity of anti-freeze, which resulted in consumer panic buying which allowed companies to raise prices and to keep them high.
I should like to quote from the Toronto Star of October 30. An anti-freeze retailer, a gas station operator says:
Adjournment Debate
"It's all just one big ripoff," charges Walker who claims this year's anti-freeze shortage is as "phony" as last year's energy crisis.
"We are being dictated to by these companies that are bigger than government," he continued.
Pointing out that he bought bulk anti-freeze last year at $1.95 a gallon, Walker claims suppliers and manufacturers today are making exorbitant profits while the service station operators are being "crucified".
We know that there is no scarcity but we are still confronted with anti-freeze ranging from $7 to $12 per gallon.
In view of the facts I have outlined, and in view of an inquiry launched by the Minister of Financial Institutions in Quebec, which also concludes that an artificial scarcity was created, will the minister launch an investigation under the terms of the Combines Investigation Act, to prohibit such blatant profiteering by anti-freeze producers in this country? Will the minister act to protect consumers?

speakeroldname: Mr. Norman A. Cafik (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: CONSUMER AFFAIRS-PRICE OF ANTI-FREEZE-REASON FOR INCREASED MARKUP AND POSSIBILITY OF PROFITEERING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes) has built up an impressive case to show the extent of the increase in price of anti-freeze in this country. He did a good job in demonstrating differentials in prices across this country. Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs investigations confirm, without specifying particular instances, that the substance of the hon. member's information is correct. In our investigations last week we found that a gallon of anti-freeze in the Toronto area sold for as little as $5.80 a gallon and for as much as $12 a gallon. Clearly the price differential is large.
When the department is asked how it justifies such increases, the answer is that we, in the department, do not justify them. We do not say that we feel they are justified. The simple fact is that we lack the legislative base for dealing with what may be termed profiteering. An antiprofiteering bill was introduced in the last parliament but was not passed. The election intervened. Another similar bill will be introduced in the present session of parliament and will deal with that question.
Touching on the Combines Investigation Act and evidence of violations under that act taking place, let me say that this is a matter of judgment. As I said in responding to the question immediately prior to this one, the department is not in a position to comment whether it is presently engaged in investigations under the act or whether it plans to become so engaged. As I said before, if any Canadian obtains evidence of price fixing, or of collusion in the market place which violates the spirit and content of the Combines Investigation Act, members of this House and of the general public can be assured that the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs will take appropriate action to see that Canadians are protected by laws under which we work and which have been passed by parliament.

Mr. Speaker, in my question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. 1350

November 14, 1974
Adjournment Debate
Lalonde) today I assumed that the minister had been informed of a shutdown last week of most Quebec pharmacies. They were showing support for a proposed bylaw which could drive discount drugstores out of business. It was against this background that the minister introduced Bill S-9 which, incidentally, passed Senate third reading yesterday.
Let me state at once that my question suggesting the revision or withdrawal of Bill S-9 is in no way a criticism of the principal intent of the bill. Putting quantitative ingredient information on the label is desirable. The real concern is the ability to sell products presently registered under the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act in non-pharmacies in Canada. There is no assurance that non-drug sales will be permitted after repeal of the act. Assurances have been given that the pharmacy acts of the various provinces will be amended to allow proprietary medicines to be sold in stores other than pharmacies. But this assurance may not be fulfilled, and it niay be the intent never to fulfill it.
The federal Department of National Health and Welfare has no direct authority over the pharmacy acts of the various provinces. Knowing the concern of the pharmacists about having any medicines sold in non-pharmacy outlets, the provinces may be reluctant to pass the enabling legislation.
The discount store has had a major influence on proprietary medicine prices. The consumer interest in this vital matter must be recognized, not only as it affects the price which the consumer must pay but also in the ready accessibility which is afforded by the freer sale of any product.
The consumer must be able to obtain full information concerning the use of his medicine, and the public must have a free choice to pay the lowest possible price.
It is my firm belief that the federal government has the duty and responsibility to exercise to the full its powers and authority in the interests of the Canadian people as a whole. That is why I questioned the minister's answer today. I again ask him how he can reconcile the undoubtedly good primary thrust of Bill S-9 and its unfortunate possible future implications for the consumer?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the hon. member for
Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) for his interest in this particular subject and his well-known concern for the interests of consumers. It is a concern which is shared by most members of this House, expecially as it deals with the price of drugs to Canadian citizens. He mentioned the great advantages that had resulted to consumers from discount drugstores in some provinces. His worry that they may disappear is certainly well understood.
I wish to stress that the question of legislation authorizing such drug sales is a matter which comes under the responsibility of the provinces at the present time. It will remain under the responsibility of the provinces after passage of Bill S-9, if the House decides to approve that bill.
I have had several contacts and communications with my provincial colleagues over the past year in connection with this bill, particularly at the federal-provincial conference of health ministers in February, 1974. My colleagues unanimously agreed that we could repeal the PPM Act and substitute another bill which would provide for greater disclosure than exists at the present time.
There was a meeting on October 3, 1974, of the Registrars of Pharmacy of the various provinces. Particular consideration was given to the changes that would be required in provincial pharmacy legislation to accommodate the repeal of the PPM Act. I might point out to the hon. member that a resolution was passed unanimously at that meeting supporting the actions taken by the Health Protection Branch in the matter of repeal of the PPM Act.
During the discussions it was agreed that there was adequate time to effect the changes required in provincial legislation since they were considered to be minimal. In general, present provincial legislation allows for the sale of proprietary medicines in non-pharmacy outlets by referring to products registered under the PPM Act. It is anticipated that the major change required will be to refer to the new regulations concerning proprietary medicines under the Food and Drugs Act.
Bill S-9 provides that the bill will come into effect in July 1976. That allows a year and a half to ensure transition. There should be no reason why any province has not passed the necessary legislation in the meantime. I might point out that provision will be made for progressive implementation of the act in the interim period.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 10:25 p.m.
